text: Prentiss’s flat was the parlour floor of a house on Stuyvesant Street, ten minutes’ walk east. The cold had got into the gutters and the gutters had given up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The house was old and proud of it, with a carpet on the stairs held down by brass rods, and every rod shone. Somebody polished them. Somebody, I’d guess, who also kept an eye on who came and went, though nobody in this house was paid to. ¶ The door had no mark on it. Prentiss stood in the parlour doorway and looked at the place where Duchess ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping. A framed sampler on the wall said Bless This House in red cross-stitch. ¶ If she went at ten or eleven, the house had been empty, and anyone who’d heard him at the Thalia had known where the key was. That was the room, more or less. It was a big room.

Midnight. Two rooms over a Chinese laundry on Mulberry Street. My knuckle had split open again, the same place as last month, and frost had crept across the window glass from the inside. A woman came up the stairs after midnight. ¶ She stood a moment inside the door with her gloves in one hand. They were new enough that a price tag was still folded down inside one cuff. She hadn’t noticed, or hadn’t cared to. She was in her thirties, dressed for an office she didn’t have. ◆ She had the look of someone who did her business standing up, on a curb, with one eye on the street. ¶ “My name is Ilse Hauck,” she said. “My sister was married to Isidore Sirkin. He’s dead.” ¶ I let her sit before I asked anything. ¶ “Sirkin was a buildings inspector,” she said. “He could close a building with a signature, and he had closed two. You can imagine how many friends that made him. They found him in his walk-up. Crowninshield found him, at half past eleven. She rents from him.” ¶ “And the police?” ¶ “They wrote it down as a fall and closed the book on it.” Her mouth went thin. “The door was locked. The windows were painted shut. There’s one key to that walk-up, and it hangs on a hook at the third floor, and this morning it was on the hook. The coroner says between eight and half past. That’s not a fall. That’s somebody with a key.” ¶ “Why me, and not the precinct again?” ¶ “Because the precinct is finished with it, and I’d like it to stay finished in public.” She turned the gloves over. “I want it found. I don’t want it said. I’m paying for both.” ¶ ◆ She traded stocks on the street for men who would rather not be seen doing it themselves. She knew what quiet was worth to a customer, and she was pricing it for herself. ¶ “Where would you start?” ¶ “Steinbach. He blamed Sirkin for losing his business. He said so to anyone who’d listen.” ¶ She put a hundred dollars on the desk and waited for me to pick it up before she let go of the edge of it.

Tried to get you at your hotel but they told me you hadn’t been in.” ¶ He wasn’t looking well this morning, but under his glad-handing he seemed, for a change, genuinely glad to see me. ¶ As I sat down one of his phones rang. He put the receiver to his ear, said, “Yes?” listened for a moment, said, “You better go out there yourself, Mac,” and had to make two attempts to get the receiver back on its prong before he succeeded. His face had gone a little doughy, but his voice was almost normal as he told me: ¶ “Lew Yard’s been knocked off, shot coming down his front steps just now.” ¶ “Any details?” I asked while I cursed myself for having pulled Dick Foley away from Painter Street an hour too soon. That was a tough break. ¶ Noonan shook his head, staring at his lap. ¶ “Shall we go out and look at the remains?” I suggested, getting up. ¶ He neither got up nor looked up.

He stopped, pretending interest in the shape the red puddle was taking. I knew pain had stopped him, but I knew he would go on talking as soon as he got himself in hand. He meant to die as he had lived, inside the same tough shell. Talking could be torture, but he wouldn’t stop on that account, not while anybody was there to see him. He was Reno Starkey who could take anything the world had without batting an eye, and he would play it out that way to the end. ¶ “I got tired of waiting,” he went on after a moment. “I hit her door and asked how come. She takes me in, telling me there’s nobody there. I’m doubtful, but she swears she’s alone, and we go back in the kitchen. Knowing her, I’m beginning to think maybe it’s me and not Whisper that’s being trapped.” ¶ Mickey came in, telling us he had phoned for an ambulance. ¶ Reno used the interruption to rest his voice, and then continued with his story:

“Gabrielle had hardly been born before I began planning what I should some day do; and when she was nearly five I did it. Maurice’s pistol, a small one, was kept in a locked drawer high in a chiffonier. I unlocked the drawer, unloaded the pistol, and taught Gabrielle an amusing little game. I would lie on Lily’s bed, pretending to sleep. The child would push a chair to the chiffonier, climb up on it, take the pistol from the drawer, creep over to the bed, put the muzzle of the pistol to my head, and press the trigger. When she did it well, making little or no noise, holding the pistol correctly in her tiny hands, I would reward her with candy, cautioning her against saying anything about the game to her mother or to anyone else, as we were going to surprise her mother with it.

His face was composed, as if he were sleeping. His arms were straight down at his sides. His clothes were not rumpled, though his coat and vest were unbuttoned. His shirt was all blood. There were four holes in his shirtfront, all alike, all the size and shape that the weapon the girl had given me would have made. No blood was coming from his wounds now, but when I put a hand on his forehead I found it not quite cold. There was blood on the altar steps, and on the floor below, where his noseglasses, unbroken, on the end of their black ribbon, lay. ¶ I straightened up and swung the beam of my light into the girl’s face. She blinked and squinted, but her face showed nothing except that physical discomfort. ¶ “You killed him?” I asked. ¶ Young Collinson came out of his trance to bawl: “No.” ¶ “Shut up,” I told him, stepping closer to the girl, so he couldn’t wedge himself between us. “Did you?” I asked her again. ¶ “Are you surprised?” she inquired quietly. “You were there when my stepmother told of the cursed Dain blood in me, and of what it had done and would do to me and those who touched me. Is this,” she asked, pointing at the dead man, “anything you should not have expected?”

I worked the automatic’s trigger, pumping six more bullets into his face and body. I saw them go in. And he came on steadily, showing in no way that he was conscious of them. His eyes and face were stern, but not angry. When he was close to me the knife in his hand went up high above his head. That’s no way to fight with a knife; but he wasn’t fighting: he was bringing retribution to me, and he paid as little attention to my attempts to stop him as a parent does to those of a small child he’s punishing. ¶ I was fighting. When the knife, shining over our heads, started down I went in under it, bending my right forearm against his knife-arm, driving the dagger in my left hand at his throat. I drove the heavy blade into his throat, in till the hilt’s cross stopped it. Then I was through.

He learned the truth about it when, surprising Fitzstephan in further attempts to make Gabrielle, as Fitzstephan put it, listen to reason, he had got into a three-cornered row with the pair of them. Leggett now began to understand what sort of a woman he was married to. Fitzstephan was no longer invited to the Leggett house, but kept in touch with Alice and waited his time. ¶ His time came when Upton arrived with his demand for blackmail. Alice went to Fitzstephan for advice. He gave it to her, poisonously. He urged her to handle Upton herself, concealing his demand, his knowledge of the Leggett past, from Leggett. He told her she should above all else continue to keep her knowledge of Leggett’s Central American and Mexican history concealed from him, a valuable hold on him now that he hated her because of what she’d taught the girl. Giving Upton the diamonds, and faking the burglary evidence, were Fitzstephan’s ideas. Poor Alice didn’t mean anything to him: he didn’t care what happened to her so long as he could ruin Leggett and get Gabrielle.

Spade, coming around the corner from the elevator at a few minutes past six in the morning, saw yellow light glowing through the frosted glass of his office door. He halted abruptly, set his lips together, looked up and down the corridor, and advanced to the door with swift quiet strides. ¶ He put his hand on the knob and turned it with care that permitted neither rattle nor click. He turned the knob until it would turn no farther: the door was locked. Holding the knob still, he changed hands, taking it now in his left hand. With his right hand he brought his keys out of his pocket, carefully, so they could not jingle against one another. He separated the office-key from the others and, smothering the others together in his palm, inserted the office-key in the lock. The insertion was soundless. He balanced himself on the balls of his feet, filled his lungs, clicked the door open, and went in. ¶ Effie Perine sat sleeping with her head on her forearms, her forearms on her desk. She wore her coat and had one of Spade’s overcoats wrapped cape-fashion around her.

The room was a large one, and heavy with the thick hangings and bulky horsehair furniture of a generation ago. I burned the cigar the old man had given me, and slumped comfortably down in my chair, letting them run on, putting in a word or two whenever they turned to me. I didn’t expect to get any information here; but I was comfortable, and the cigar was a good one. Another complication: I am neither young enough nor old enough to get feverish over every woman who doesn’t make me think being blind isn’t so bad. But there is something else. Long ago men hunted and fished to keep alive. They fought with animals and sat with empty stomachs staring at the water, not in quest of Nirvanas but of fish. So now, after ages and ages have passed, there is left a vague memory of this in the minds of these fishermen. This memory makes them still feel a certain thrill in the business of pursuit. Even as they sit, stoical and inanimate, forgetful of unpaid bills, unfinished and never-to-be-finished plans, there comes this curious thrill. A mouth tugs at the little minnow. The pole jerks electrically in the hand. Something alive is on the hook. And the fisherman for an instant recovers his past. He is Ab, fighting with an evening meal off the coast of Wales, two glacial periods ago. His body quivers, his muscles set, his eyes flash.

Mrs. Rodjezke had come to the lake to cool off. The idea of going for a swim had been in her head for at least three years. She had always been able to overcome it, but this time somehow it had got the better of her and she had moved almost blindly toward the water front. ¶ “I will get a rest in the water,” she thought. ¶ But now on the beach Mrs. Rodjezke found it difficult to rest. The dishes weren’t washed in the kitchen home. The clothes needed changing on the beds. And other things. Lots of other things. ¶ Mrs. Rodjezke sighed as the shouts of the bathers floated by her ears. The sun had almost gone down and the lake looked dull. Faintly colored clouds were beginning to hide the water. It was no use. Mrs. Rodjezke couldn’t rest. She sat and stared harder at the lake. Yes, there was something to do. Before it got too dark. Something very important to do. And it wasn’t right not to do it. The scrubwoman sighed again and put her hand against her side. The burn had dropped to there. It had also gone into her head. But that was a thing which must be forgotten. Mrs. Rodjezke had learned how to forget it during the eight years.

“Do you remember the Leggett mystery?” he inquired doubtfully. “I guess that was before your time. I was only a patrolman then. Old Leggett had a tobacco jar made out of a human skull, and that’s how they found out he killed his wife. It was her skull. It come out one evening when he brought his bride home. You know, he got married again after killin’ the first one. And they was having a party and the new bride said she didn’t want that skull around in her house. Old Leggett got mad and said he wouldn’t part with that skull for love or money. So when he was to work one day she threw the skull into the ash can, and when old Leggett come home and saw the skull missing he swore like the devil and come down to the station to swear out a warrant for his wife’s arrest, chargin’ her with disorderly conduct. He carried on so that one of the boys got suspicious and went out to the house with him and they found the skull in the ash can, and old Leggett began to weep over it. So one of the boys asked him, naturally, whose skull it was. He said it wasn’t a skull no more, but a tobacco jar. And they asked him where he’d got it. And he begun to lie so hard that they tripped him up and finally he said it was his first wife’s skull, and he was hung shortly afterward. You see, if you give me time I could remember something like that for a story.

They will go with him. The miser who has hidden away his gold, the widow and her two orphans, the hungry ones and despairing ones, they will all go back with him. ¶ One comes out of the theater with a strange sense of understanding. The dead have spoken to one. It is never to be forgotten. The youth that was ripped to pieces in the trenches reached out his limp arms across a row of west side footlights and left a cry echoing in one’s heart: “My unlived days! My uneaten bread! My uncounted years! They lie in a little corner waiting and no one comes to them.” ¶ Propaganda? Yes, a curious undertone of propaganda. The war propaganda of the dead, older than the fall of Liege by a hundred centuries. The primitive propaganda of the world mourning for its lost ones. ¶ You will see the play, perhaps. Or you will wait until it is translated some day. But this month the west side is aglow with the genius of Sholom Ash and with the interpretative genius of Aaron Teitelbaum, who plays the dead man in uniform and who directed the production. I know of no performance today that rivals his.

A dark afternoon with summer thunder in the sky. The fan-shaped skyscrapers spread a checkerboard of window lights through the gloom. It rains. People seem to grow vaguely elate on the dark wet pavements. They hurry along, their eyes saying to one another, “We have something in common. We are all getting wet in the rain.” The crowd is no longer quite so enigmatic a stranger to itself. An errand boy from Market Street advances with leaps through the downpour, a high chant on his lips, “It’s raining.it’s raining.” The rain mutters and the pavements, like darkened mirrors, grow alive with impressionistic cartoons of the city.

The newspaper man watched him. As he stood looking after him some one tapped him on the shoulder. He turned. “Specs” McLaughlin of the detective bureau. “Specs” rubbed his chin contemplatively and smiled. ¶ “Know that guy?” ¶ “Who?” ¶ “No; just bumped into him. How come?” ¶ “You might have got a story out of him,” “Specs” grinned. “That’s George Cook. Just let out of the Joliet pen this morning. Served fourteen years. Quite a yarn at the time. For killing a pal in the Wellington hotel over some dame. I guess that was before your time, though. He just landed in town this noon.” ¶ The detective rubbered into the moving crowd. ¶ “I’m sort of keeping an eye on him,” he said, and hurried on.

This was the woman I was to help, the one who had neglected her family, played too near the fire, and now would give her soul to be kneeling by that little crib at home, a free woman, one who saw nothing unless it. ¶ But Josey was talking. ¶ “We’ll make a night of it, you and I, Stacey. You know no one and J, well, I’ll cut and cut’ Her hair brushed my cheek; her dancing eyes looked into mine, but I shook my head. ¶ “Not to-night, Josey,” I said. ‘“Business, an appointment. Until eleven.”

A light was fairly safe. If the coffee-maker had one, why not me? I closed the window, pulled down the shade and, holding my revolver in my right hand, slipped my electric torch open with my left. A stab of yellow. A good sized kitchen, this. A door with a key in it, which evidently opened to the cellar, also a heavy swinging door that led to the dining room, or more likely the pantry, for the house was large and old. ¶ I was cold and chilled myself. After ducking my head through the swinging door, which proved my idea about the pantry, I stepped back and, taking a cup from the table, gulped down the steaming black coffee. On the table, too, was a pint bottle of whisky. That must have been what the cook meant when he said he put something in the coffee besides his finger. Good! I like to clear little things like that up. But I passed the whisky. I needed a clear head, a keen eye, and fingers of steel. ¶ The thrill of the thing was on me as I passed into the pantry, smothering my light, and poked a head out the other swinging door. The past was sweeping back and guiding every movement; the glamour of the old days was ringing in my ears.

Some feel a trembling of the whole body afterward, a reaction of weakness that knocks one completely. I didn’t. There was just a deadly calm, and a brain as clear as a mountain stream, though racing as rapidly, too. ¶ One thing stood out, overshadowed all the others. Josey Mears had been an actress. Was she still one? Had she played a part that afternoon? Certainly, unless Josey was actually married, this blackmail was a useless farce without the help of the girl. ¶ The creature on the floor had crawled to the door, pulled himself erect and stood there, leaning against the casement, bracing his body as he clutched spasmodically for the knob. Twice he opened his mouth to speak, twice he raised his hand and pointed a finger at me. Whether his tongue was too dry, or there was something in my face that stopped him, I don’t know. ¶ But he said nothing, stood so a moment, found the knob and passed out into the hall. I heard him fumbling at the front door, followed quickly, and gave him my parting shot.

If I could play the part of an innocent fool who had just happened in, well, even the powerful hand of the Black Circle would hardly take human life needlessly. This man was thinking things out. I could see the indecision in his every movement. The desire to kill in that finger that tightened about the trigger, and yet he hesitated. The Black Circle doubtless planned for one killing, not two. ¶ “Where did you get that gun?” he asked suddenly, and his head came up like an animal who gets the scent. Perhaps he had searched this room before I did, would know if I lied. But I tried it anyway. ¶ “In the closet there.” I jerked a thumb toward the still open closet door. ‘On the floor, back in the corner, my foot kicked against it.” ¶ His eyes gleamed the brighter through the slits, but I could not get what he was thinking. ¶ “Your name, and how did you come here?”

“So, Mr. Burglar.” His hand came slowly up toward my gun. “T’ll take that, I think.” And I was thinking, too, thinking fast. If I threatened to kill him if he moved, what then? Under certain circumstances that might go all right. But I didn’t know who was behind me, and besides, the street outside was thick with the police. We’d look a pretty picture standing there, if the police broke in the doors or followed a servant to that one lighted room. ¶ Already I had gone too far. I should have faced it out in the house of death, told a straight story. Now, well, I shrugged my shoulders. I’d have to make the best of it, perhaps be held for a double murder. ¶ The fingers of the little man wound gently about my gun and slipped it from my grasp. Still the hard pressure in my back and the deadly silence, never a threat, never a word, Just the feel of a prodding gun. ¶ “Good.” The man spun my revolver around on his finger. Pretended familiarity there, but I didn’t wish to see him commit suicide, or perhaps send a bullet crashing through my head. So I warned him. ¶ “That gun is keyed to a hair’s pressure,” I told him. “A bit of a jerk to that swing and.”

since that first night I have not carried a pistol, now I’m doubtful.” ¶ So was I. That was something to think over. My idea was to hide in the house, listen in on the conversation, much as I had done with Mrs. Clayburn, attack suddenly, in the same manner, too. Yet, in case of sudden surprise, two guns were better than one. After some discussion it was decided that he had best keep his gun. ¶ If they searched him and found it before I acted, his excuse for carrying it would be a good one. Ten thousand dollars on a lonely road, in the dark hours of the morning. Good. I held out a hand and took his as we parted. ¶ Together we raised our eyes and looked at the dismal building, outlined against the blackness of the night. Nota light in a window, not a moving shadow upon the whole countryside. ¶ “You can count on me absolutely, Mr. Townsend,” I told him as he turned toward the house. “If they’re hidden inside, if they surprise you in the dark, it doesn’t matter. If you don’t signal me I’ll come to you anyway, come if I have to crash in the front door.” And I meant it.

There followed a half-century of unprecedented expansion. Money was needed for railroads, telegraph lines, factories, for building cities over night and exploiting the resources of the West. Financial titans arose: Jay Gould, Jim Fisk, Daniel Drew, Jim Hill, E. H. Harriman, and the elder J. P. Morgan. After Gould, Fisk, and Drew, with the help of bribed New York legislators, had succeeded in their struggle with Commodore Vanderbilt for the control of the Erie Railroad, Gould and Fisk conceived the plan of cornering the gold market, counting on the United States Treasury not to sell from its gold reserve. But when the price of gold reached 162 on Black Friday (September 24, 1869), President Grant ordered the Treasury to sell, breaking the corner. The panic of 1869 resulted, followed by a depression which lasted ten years. Banks, brokers, merchants suspended business; nearly one hundred railroads failed, and the Stock Exchange closed its doors.

The building, opened in 1914, cost about twelve million dollars. The municipally owned and operated Radio Station, Wnyc, on the twenty-fifth floor, broadcasts no commercial programs; performers are supplied by government agencies and educational institutions. The Municipal Reference Library, on the twenty-second floor, a branch of the New York Public Library, contains documents, pamphlets, maps, directories, and reports from all important cities. On the second floor, across the hall from the marriage license bureau, is the Marriage Chapel, a sunny room decorated with flowered wallpaper and potted palms.

The National Biscuit Company’s Plant on Fourteenth Street near Tenth Avenue is the largest factory in the neighborhood. It has about forty-six acres of floor space and employs several thousand workers.

Marble Hill, Inwood’s little neighbor to the northeast, is tied to Manhattan Island by the bridge over which Broadway crosses the Harlem. The hill was called Papirinemen by the Indians, meaning “a place parcelled out.” Old marble quarries gave it the name most commonly used, but occasionally it is referred to as Kingsbridge, a name derived from a bridge, the first across the river, that Frederick Philipse built in 1693. Indignant farmers resented paying toll to Philipse, a wealthy Dutch Colonial, and erected the free Farmers’ Bridge. General Washington’s troops used both crossings in their retreat to White Plains after the battle on Harlem Heights.

When Williamsbridge was incorporated as a village in 1888, it included the villages of Olinville Number One, Olinville Number Two, Wakefield, and Jerome. The same year, the large oval Gun Hill Reservoir (no longer used) was put into service. ¶ About 1890, a factory that had been established for the manufacture of imitation Gobelin tapestries attracted a number of French tapestry weavers who settled along the Bronx River. Several French restaurants were opened in the colony, and these became popular resorts.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. The coffee I’d made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head. ¶ Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely. My visitor knocked once, came in, and sat down like somebody who’d been rehearsing it on the stairs. ¶ “Somebody has taken my Pomeranian,” Schilling said. “Duchess. Gone from her cushion by the radiator, just like that.” ¶ “I was at my sister’s all evening, and the flat was locked,” she said. “Mrs. Callahan keeps the spare key on a nail in the hall at the Delmonico rooms, where anybody who comes in can see it.” ¶ “And when did Duchess go?” ¶ She had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the A&P Gypsies, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want her badly enough to take her?” ¶ “Start with Alfano,” she said. “She owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ She hesitated, then went on. “Margolis, a cab driver, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill. And Bernstein, a cafeteria cashier, is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a Pomeranian with papers fetches.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Schilling said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where Duchess is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and west to the Delmonico rooms, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Callahan was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bernstein was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ The spare key lived on the nail in the hall here. That settled where I was going. ¶ A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

I took the chair opposite Alfano and kept my hands where she could see them, on the tablecloth. ¶ “Mrs. Callahan has you at the Delmonico rooms at eight. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” She put down what she was holding and gave me her attention. ¶ “I was home at the Delmonico rooms at eight, with Bernstein and Doyle. Then at nine I went to the chop house for coffee and pie, with Shapiro. Come ten, I turned in early, home at the Delmonico rooms, on my own.” ¶ Alfano said home at ten. Mrs. Callahan had Bernstein and Doyle at the Delmonico rooms at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ It turned out Shapiro was at a table by the wall, behind a menu. ¶ The samovar went on steaming at the end of the counter, the only thing in the room in no hurry at all. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Alfano had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Callahan’s list said otherwise. Bernstein was at the Delmonico rooms at ten; Mrs. Callahan said so. Margolis hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ I could put it to Alfano now. Or I could find out first who Mulcahy had seen at the chop house. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Mimi,” Hargrove said. “My Persian. She’s gone from the window seat.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I sat in the Velvet Room from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did Mimi go missing?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past ten.” ¶ “Anybody you can think of who’d want Mimi?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Havemeyer,” Hargrove said. “She stood at my elbow at the Velvet Room the whole time, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a Persian with papers fetches.” ¶ He hesitated, then went on. “Doyle, a switchboard operator, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Mimi was worth. And Pickering, a sewing-machine operator, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

It was a fair few blocks to the Velvet Room, west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. Behind the bar a moose head with one glass eye looked out over the bottles, having seen it all and liked none of it. ¶ Quill was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Pickering was standing at the bar with her coat over her arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

Kowalski’s lay a couple of blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Havemeyer answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. Colquitt was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Pickering had said she was here at nine, and that Havemeyer was with her at the Velvet Room at eight. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

It was a long walk from there to the Coffin flat, uptown and east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Coffin parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax. A framed sampler on the wall said Bless This House in red cross-stitch. ¶ Coffin showed me in and stood by the place where Duchess belonged, holding Duchess’s dish as if it might be wanted any minute. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If she went at ten, she went after the supper, and everybody at the supper had known the way in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Sirkin. ¶ I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ She asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “I was home at Mrs. Nagy’s from eight through ten. At eight it was just me; Petrosino was there at nine; at ten it was just me. Eleven o’clock I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning, by myself.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Sirkin said home, here at Mrs. Nagy’s. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ The one to ask was the foreman at the print shop, who’d been there all night. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

The Orpheum lay a few blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Mulcahy stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Cheatham was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Weisglass stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Petrosino sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it. ¶ Cheatham had been at Coffin’s at eight, for the supper. Sirkin had said Petrosino was with her at her place at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Mulcahy. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Cheatham had told me the Orpheum at ten, and Mulcahy’s list said otherwise. It was time she heard about the other one. I found her page in my notebook and kept my thumb in it. ¶ “Let me read you something back,” I said. “You told me the Orpheum at ten. Mulcahy had Weisglass, Petrosino and Pardo at the Orpheum at ten o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ Cheatham looked hurt, the way people do when the world won’t agree to their version of it. “All right. I took it. It’s with Pardo, a man who buys things and asks nothing. I lost my job on Friday.” ¶ So Duchess was with Pardo, who was sitting ten feet away and hadn’t looked up once. That was what Coffin had paid for. ¶ The plaster mask grinned down at me the way it grins at everybody, as if we were all in on it.

I went over the table. ¶ Colquitt didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Mrs. Nagy’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. Rosenbaum had been drinking with a friend, or with somebody who passed for one. ¶ So the chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Rosenbaum had been at Mrs. Nagy’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Rosenbaum’s place yet, and papers go on talking after the one who kept them has stopped. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mosley. I put a coin on the bar so she would have a reason to come over. She came over and left the coin where it was. ¶ I asked Mosley for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. She didn’t look at the room to answer. She didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Salerno and Ellery. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Whitfield, Ellery and Rosenbaum. Nobody else at all. Ten, Bledsoe and Ellery. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Ellery hadn’t been at Mrs. Nagy’s while it was there to take. That put Bledsoe and Ellery here at ten, by her count. Colquitt had said nine or ten. Rosenbaum was at Hanley’s at nine, alive. ¶ Whitfield was right here, and his evening was still a blank in my notebook. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

I waited for a gap in Mrs. Nagy’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked Mrs. Nagy who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. ¶ She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Bledsoe and Whitfield. Nobody else. Eight, Salerno and Bledsoe. Nobody else at all. Nine, Bledsoe. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Salerno, Bledsoe and Whitfield had been here earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking. Mrs. Nagy had Whitfield here at seven, same as he said. I wrote down what the list had at ten, the hour that mattered: nobody. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Salerno had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Nagy’s list said otherwise. It was time to say so to his face. I turned back to him with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody. ¶ “One thing,” I said to him. “You said home at ten. Mrs. Nagy had nobody at Mrs. Nagy’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ He let out a breath he’d been keeping since I sat down. “All right. I wasn’t at Mrs. Nagy’s. I was at Sokol’s, in the back, putting a nickel on a number. I swore I’d stopped. Ashby was there. Ask him.” ¶ That was a hole in Salerno’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, he had been at Sokol’s back room at ten, not home. ¶ It turned out Ashby was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “Fannie Rosenbaum,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Albrecht Obermann’s sister-in-law, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ The dead man was a moneylender. Doyle, who’d come to settle a bet, found the body in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair. She took it, and held her hat on her knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ She had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “The police surgeon puts it at nine or ten o’clock, by the warmth of him.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was the Kit Kat, the same as every night,” she said. “The usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “There’s a letter from Doyle in the desk,” she said. “It was on top, and I didn’t look any further. He owed Obermann four hundred dollars.” ¶ Rosenbaum put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money. It was the first good news of the night, and I was making the most of it.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. I went through the papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Vitale: a court transcript, his own testimony against her brother. Bellucci: a file he’d kept on her, thick enough to matter. Ellery: a column of payments, every month for years, and her name at the top. Doyle: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the chloral, and that was at Mrs. Nagy’s. ¶ Rosenbaum had pointed me at Doyle, and that was worth the walk to the Kit Kat. ¶ The calendar by the stove was still on last month. Nobody was going to turn it now.

Doyle had said he was here at eight and ten, and Lefkowitz had been here to see who came and went. ¶ I asked him for a minute, and he gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. I asked him who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. ¶ He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Vitale and Ellery. Nobody else. Eight, Doyle, Ellery and Obermann. Nobody else at all. Nine, Obermann. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Vitale and Ellery. Nobody else.” ¶ Doyle said the Kit Kat at ten. The doorkeeper had Vitale and Ellery here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Lefkowitz had no reason to be the wrong one. Ellery hadn’t been at Mrs. Nagy’s while it was there to take. Rosenbaum had said nine or ten. Obermann was at the Kit Kat at nine, alive. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Rosenbaum had said nine or ten, and Obermann was at the Kit Kat at nine, alive. The chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Ellery hadn’t. Vitale was at the Kit Kat at ten; Lefkowitz said so. Doyle had told me the Kit Kat at ten, and Lefkowitz’s list said otherwise. Ellery was at the Kit Kat at ten; Lefkowitz said so. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

It was no distance to the Eagle club office: round the corner, and there it was. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The back office of the Eagle Social Club was where the club did the business it didn’t do in the front room. There were a lot of chairs for an office, and not much paper. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Callahan was at the steward’s desk, sorting the club’s letters into pigeonholes. ¶ A club steward knows every member by the back of the head, and every visitor by the fact that she doesn’t. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I got as near to Bellucci as manners allowed and said my name. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” She smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “I was home at seven. Eight o’clock I went to Mrs. Nagy’s to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Vitale was there at eight; Vitale and Ellery were there at nine. Then at ten I went home, because my feet hurt. At seven and ten I was on my own.” ¶ Bellucci said home at ten. Ellery passed her on Hester Street at ten. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. The rest held where I could check it: Vitale had her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight and at Mrs. Nagy’s at nine, same as she said. ¶ The kettle on the gas ring was cold. Nobody was going to offer me tea in that flat.

I went over Shapiro’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Hargrove waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time she shifted her weight. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from the Delmonico rooms. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. He had been drinking with a friend, or with somebody who passed for one. ¶ So the chloral came from the Delmonico rooms, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Shapiro had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Quill. I went over to her and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” She counted it off on her fingers, and ran out of fingers before she ran out of night. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Lindemann and Ruggiero. Nobody else. Eight, Lindemann, Tramonti, Broadnax and Ruggiero. Nobody else at all. Nine, Lindemann, Tramonti and Ruggiero. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Ruggiero and Hanrahan. Nobody else. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ I wrote down what Mrs. Quill had at nine and ten, the hours that mattered: Ruggiero at both, Lindemann and Tramonti at nine and Hanrahan at ten. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

The Thalia was a good walk uptown and west. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ I went in at the Thalia, a Yiddish theater on the Bowery. The play was over, but the stage still had its painted village up, a little wooden town waiting under one work light for the next performance. The lobby carpet was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats. ¶ Lanza stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. Lindemann, in a grey fedora, was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. He smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept his gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. ¶ Broadnax had said she was here at nine, and that Lindemann was with her at her place at ten. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Lanza. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Getting to Sokol’s back room meant a few blocks east. A newspaper went by in the gutter. It might have been the same one. It was making better time than I was. ¶ I went round to the back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where a nickel bet on a three-figure number bought you a reason to get up tomorrow. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Tramonti, with a bandaged hand, was at a table by the wall, watching the room the way people watch rooms they shouldn’t be in. Young and tidy and a little tired, he still had the mark of the headset band pressed into his hair. ¶ Lindemann had said Tramonti was with him at the Delmonico rooms at nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. The coffee I’d made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head. ¶ Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely. My visitor knocked once, came in, and sat down like somebody who’d been rehearsing it on the stairs. ¶ “Somebody has taken my Persian,” Mrs. Pomerantz said. “Mimi. Gone from the window seat, just like that.” ¶ “I was at my sister’s all evening, and the flat was locked,” she said. “Wojcik keeps the spare key on a nail in the hall at the flats over Lipsky’s, where anybody who comes in can see it.” ¶ “And when did Mimi go?” ¶ She had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want her badly enough to take her?” ¶ “Ask about Russo,” she said. “He owes Margolis money, and he isn’t a patient man. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She hesitated, then went on. “Miss Lowenthal, the piano teacher, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday. And Amato, the cab driver, owes Mrs. Krantz money, and she has started asking for it.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Mrs. Pomerantz said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where Mimi is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

The flats over Lipsky’s were only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The tenement over Lipsky’s was dark from the stoop to the roof, except one kitchen on the third floor where somebody was ironing a shirt for the morning. The shop window below had a card in it, EVERYTHING MUST GO, which had been saying so since the war. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was eating a sandwich of black bread and onion out of a newspaper. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Amato was eating a sandwich at the kitchen window with one eye on his cab in the street. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. Miss Lowenthal had hair in a tight bun with a pencil through it, which she uses, and a second pencil, which she forgets. ¶ “Wojcik has you at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ Miss Lowenthal took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “My evening was quiet, and I could be quiet about it, but since you ask, here it is. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight, with Russo, Amato and Teitel. Nine o’clock I had a ticket for the Lyric, and stayed the rest of the evening. Belkin was there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ So home at eight, with Russo, Amato and Teitel, which was what Wojcik had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said the Lyric. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ It turned out Belkin was three rows back with his hat over his eyes. ¶ Pinsky had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ Marking a sheet of music with tiny furious pencil notes: that was the last I saw of her.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Fritz,” Russo said. “My dachshund. He’s gone from his basket by the stove.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I had people in at eight for a birthday supper,” he said. “Kaminsky and Miss Nowak. Nobody else.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “And when did Fritz go missing?” ¶ “And I know when,” he said. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want him badly enough to take him?” ¶ “You might ask about Margolis,” he said. “He says my IOU to him is overdue, and that Fritz would square it. That’s from the woman downstairs, and she hears most things.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Miss Nowak, the switchboard operator, owes Fishel money, and he wants it by Saturday. And Kaminsky, the prizefighter, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday.” ¶ Russo counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I walked uptown and west to the Lyric. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There were pigeons in the ventilator over the gallery, who coo in the quiet parts. ¶ Pinsky was mouthing the third act from the back of the aisle. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Kaminsky was eating a raw egg out of the shell, for the strength. ¶ Kaminsky had been at Russo’s at eight, for the supper. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

Steinmetz’s lay a fair few blocks downtown. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was one curtained booth at the back, for parties who don’t want to be a party. ¶ Demos was smoothing his hair with both palms, as if it might have moved. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. Miss Kahane was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. ¶ Kaminsky had said he was here at nine. Pinsky’s list had Miss Nowak at the Lyric at nine. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

It was a few blocks from there to the Russo flat, east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Russo showed me in and stood by the place where Duchess belonged, holding Duchess’s dish as if it might be wanted any minute. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If she went at ten, she went after the christening supper, and everybody at the christening supper had known the way in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Nowak. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. She had nails painted red and bitten, both. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” Miss Nowak counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was at Russo’s at eight, for the christening supper, with Dr. Hirsch and Mrs. Greco. Around nine I left the christening supper early and went home to change, and stayed through ten. Miss Kahane and Mrs. Greco were there at nine; at ten it was just me. At eleven I went to Sokol’s to see who was in, with Miss Kahane and Mrs. Greco.” ¶ So the Russo flat at eight, with Dr. Hirsch and Mrs. Greco, which was what Russo had said. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said home at Rafferty’s. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ I wanted Sokol’s count of the night, everybody, hour by hour. ¶ Counting out change for a horse she likes: that was the last I saw of her.

Dr. Hirsch was smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window. ¶ “Sokol has you at Sokol’s at nine. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” She smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. I was at Russo’s at eight, for the christening supper, with Miss Nowak and Mrs. Greco. Nine o’clock I left the christening supper to get some air and went to Sokol’s to settle a bet, and stayed through ten. Nine, I have the cigarette. One. I make it last like a good filling. Then at eleven I went round to the back room at Wexler’s to see about a pledge. At nine, ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch said Sokol’s at ten. Sokol had Miss Kahane, Mrs. Greco and Fishel at Sokol’s at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. The rest held where I could check it: Russo had her at the Russo flat at eight, with Miss Nowak, same as she said. ¶ I didn’t sit in the chair with the short leg. I was unsteady enough. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Dr. Hirsch, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Greco were at the christening supper and knew the way in; Miss Kahane wasn’t. Dr. Hirsch had told me Sokol’s at ten, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. Miss Nowak said home at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. Miss Kahane was at Sokol’s at ten; Sokol said so. Mrs. Greco was at Sokol’s at ten; Sokol said so. And whatever it was had gone to Fishel, the bookmaker at Sokol’s at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Rafferty’s who’d been in. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

Rafferty’s was round the corner. The fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ The milk wagon was two streets off and I could hear every bottle on it, which tells you how quiet the rooming house had got. The hall smelled of soda bread and floor polish; the landlady polishes before she sleeps, so the morning finds it done. Every door upstairs had a brass number on it, and every number shone. There was the late Mr. Rafferty’s revolver, in the hall-stand drawer under the winter gloves, unloaded, she says, which is what everybody says. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was counting the umbrellas on their hooks. She had reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “I don’t need to look up. The front door has a voice of its own, and it tells me when it’s been opened by somebody who doesn’t pay rent here.” ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. Money sat in the office for once instead of a promise of it. I lit a cigarette slowly, like a man with a bank account. The cold stayed outside the glass where it belonged. ¶ Feet on the stairs, four flights of them, taken slowly. Nobody climbs four flights at midnight for the view. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “Minna Blau,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Lazar Belkin’s old sweetheart, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ The dead man was the leading man. At half past eleven, Amato, who’d come to return a borrowed book, found the body in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ I offered Mrs. Blau the chair and turned the lamp away from her. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” she said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Every night it was Steinmetz’s, earlier on,” she said. “Tonight too. The usual.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Ask about Miss Kahane,” she said. “She and Belkin had been at each other’s throats for years. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ Mrs. Blau put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

A few blocks uptown, and I was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The tenement over Lipsky’s was dark from the stoop to the roof, except one kitchen on the third floor where somebody was ironing a shirt for the morning. The shop window below had a card in it, EVERYTHING MUST GO, which had been saying so since the war. There was a row of tin mailboxes in the hall, with the names in five different hands and two crossed out. ¶ Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I went round the corner to Steinmetz’s. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Glick was polishing his derby with his sleeve. ¶ Teitel had said he was here at eight. Wojcik’s list had Miss Kahane at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.” ¶ Somebody went by with a plate of eggs, and my stomach reminded me it had been a long night.

A fair few blocks uptown, and I was at the costume room at the Lyric. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ The costume room under the Lyric’s stage was racks and racks of other people: peasants and rabbis, a czar, three brides and a dragon in two halves. A sewing machine stood under the only light with a wedding dress half mended across it, beside a box of buttons and a cold glass of tea. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Miss Moskin was eating a knish in full costume. She had big dark eyes that she knows how to use, and uses. ¶ Miss Moskin had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, she said, it was anybody’s. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “Yetta Sobel,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Hyman Glick’s friend, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ Glick was the insurance agent. Miss Moskin, who’d come to settle a bet, found the body in his own flat in the Belvedere on Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ I pointed Mrs. Sobel at the chair. She took it, and held her hat on her knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ She had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was Steinmetz’s, the same as every night,” she said. “The usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “There’s Dr. Hirsch,” she said. “I don’t like gossip, but He knew what she got up to at the card room over Feingold’s garage, and let her know he knew. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ Mrs. Sobel put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money. It was the first good news of the night, and I was making the most of it.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. I went through the papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Dr. Hirsch: a note about her and the card room over Feingold’s garage, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Mrs. Krantz: a clipping about her, with a remark pencilled across it. Miss Moskin: an IOU from Belkin, with her name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Ostrow: a sealed envelope with her name on it. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the chloral, and that was at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery. ¶ Glick had been here earlier in the evening, and that was worth the walk to Steinmetz’s. ¶ I put the room back the way I found it, which is more than whoever came before me had done.

Miss Moskin had said Dr. Hirsch was with her here at ten, so I went over. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. She had very clean hands with very short nails, and a gold wedding band she wears on a chain round her neck instead of on the hand. ¶ I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. Dr. Hirsch smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “Of course. Open wide. I mean the notebook. From seven, then, and stop me if anything hurts. I was at work, at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery from seven through eight. Eight, I start to want a cigarette, and I make myself wait till nine. Discipline. Mrs. Krantz was there at seven; Mrs. Ostrow was there at eight. Then I closed up at nine and couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, and stayed the rest of the evening. Mrs. Krantz and Glick were there at nine; Miss Moskin was there at ten.” ¶ So here at ten, which was what Miss Moskin had said. At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it. ¶ Smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window: that was the last I saw of her.

Mrs. Ostrow had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Miss Moskin’s own evening said otherwise. There was no going round it, so I didn’t. I took the chair beside her without asking. I’d stopped being company. ¶ “You told me Steinmetz’s at ten,” I said. “I wrote it down. Miss Moskin and Dr. Hirsch had each other at Steinmetz’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ She closed her eyes for a second, like somebody hearing a bill read out that she’d known was coming. “All right. A matchmaker should know better than anybody: sooner or later, everybody finds out everything. I wasn’t at Steinmetz’s. I was at the back room at Wexler’s, with Miss Nowak. Ask her.” ¶ That was a hole in Mrs. Ostrow’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, she had been at the back room at Wexler’s at ten, not at Steinmetz’s. ¶ It turned out Miss Nowak was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The bare bulb swung a little when the door went, and the shadows changed their minds.

I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ “Mrs. Krantz. I’d like your evening, if you can spare it. Where were you, and who was with you?” Mrs. Krantz counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order. At seven I went to Dr. Hirsch’s surgery about a loose filling. Eight o’clock I went home to iron a shirt for the morning. Then at nine I went to Steinmetz’s for supper, with Dr. Hirsch and Glick. Come ten, I went home. Ten, I think about the first of the month. I always think about the first of the month. Nobody was with me at eight or ten.” ¶ She said home at ten. Miss Moskin passed her on Ludlow Street at ten. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. The rest held where I could check it: Dr. Hirsch had her at Steinmetz’s at nine, with Glick, and at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery at seven, same as she said. Mrs. Sobel had said nine or ten. Glick was at Steinmetz’s at nine, alive. ¶ Drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in: that was the last I saw of her.

I went over Kaminsky’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Amato waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time he shifted his weight. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Rafferty’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. The dead man had been drinking with a friend, or with somebody who passed for one. ¶ So the chloral came from Rafferty’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Kaminsky had been at Rafferty’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Rafferty. ¶ She was saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open. I asked her who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. ¶ She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Seven, I take my chair and the mending, and the house knows I’m on. Seven o’clock, Russo, Mrs. Blau and Miss Nowak. Nobody else. Eight, Doyle, Russo, Mrs. Blau and Miss Nowak. Nobody else at all. Nine, Doyle, Mrs. Blau and Miss Nowak. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Miss Kahane and Mrs. Blau. Nobody else. Nobody gets past the basket. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ At nine and ten, when it counted, Mrs. Rafferty had Mrs. Blau at both, Doyle and Miss Nowak at nine and Miss Kahane at ten. ¶ Pouring tea nobody asked for: that was the last I saw of her.

Sokol’s was a couple of blocks uptown and west. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ The bakery half of Sokol’s had woken up and the bar half had gone to bed. The ovens had the shop warm enough to steam the window, and the first trays of rolls were coming out. The door marked FLOUR was shut, with a sack of real flour leaning on it as an alibi. There was a back shelf of bottles with good labels and the same rye in all of them. ¶ Sokol was counting glasses onto a towel. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Miss Nowak, in a green hat, was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. ¶ Kaminsky had been here earlier in the evening. Russo had said Miss Nowak was with him at his place at ten. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Getting to the curtained booth at the back at Steinmetz’s meant a couple of blocks downtown and east. A newspaper went by in the gutter. It might have been the same one. It was making better time than I was. ¶ The curtained booth at the back of Steinmetz’s was a table for four behind green velvet on brass rings, with its own lamp, its own coat hook and its own bell to ring for service, so that nobody ever need see who was behind it. A menu on the table had been folded into a little boat, and then a second, smaller boat. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Doyle, in a grey fedora, was shaking hands with a man who didn’t offer his. He was a florid man in a derby and a checked waistcoat, with a carnation in his buttonhole that the alderman pays for. ¶ Miss Nowak had said Doyle was with her at her place at nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor was already diagnosing the room, the stairs and my lack of a secretary before he sat down. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Doyle said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ “I was at the pictures all evening, and the flat was locked,” he said. “The spare key lives in the sugar tin on the kitchen shelf at Kowalski’s. Mrs. Kowalski keeps it there, and everybody who drops in knows it.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “The man below heard the door go just after the ten o’clock el went by; he sets his watch by it.” ¶ “Who’d want it badly enough to take it?” ¶ “Look at Marchetti,” he said. “He was in at Kowalski’s this evening, where the spare key is kept. Who does that? And he lost his job on Friday, and asked me what the cigarette case was worth.” ¶ Then he went quieter, though there was nobody else in the room. “Wehrle, a cafeteria cashier, says the cigarette case was promised to her by my late father. And Ellery, an insurance agent, is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the cigarette case would pawn for.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” Doyle said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

It was a few blocks to Kowalski’s, downtown and east. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Ellery was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ The spare key lived in the sugar tin here. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

I got as near to Marchetti as manners allowed and said my name. “Mrs. Kowalski has you at Kowalski’s at nine. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ Marchetti put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “I was at the Blue Lantern at eight, with Lefkowitz. Then at nine I went round to Kowalski’s to borrow a collar stud, with Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro. Come ten, I had a table at the Blue Lantern, alone.” ¶ So Kowalski’s at nine, with Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro, which was what Mrs. Kowalski had.
