That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said the Blue Lantern. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ It turned out Lefkowitz was at the far end of the bar, nursing something. ¶ Winslow had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ The globe was still turning overhead, throwing light at a dance floor that had stopped asking for it.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. I’d paid the landlady on my way up, and she’d counted it on the landing in front of me. The stairs felt shorter for it. The office looked the same as always, which was its own kind of relief. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. A woman came in, coat buttoned against the cold, and asked straight off what it would cost. I liked her. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Shapiro said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered her the chair. She sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I sat in the Bijou from eight until ten,” she said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ “And I know when,” she said. “The man below heard the door go just after the ten o’clock el went by; he sets his watch by it.” ¶ “Who’d want it?” ¶ “Talk to Mulcahy,” she said, without having to think about it. “He and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ Then, smaller: “Grasso, a piano teacher, says the cigarette case was promised to her by my late husband. And Stannard, a milliner, lost his job on Friday, and asked me what the cigarette case was worth.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Shapiro said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where the cigarette case is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

A few blocks downtown and east, and I was at the Bijou. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Ruggiero stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Stannard was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. ¶ An usher with a flashlight sees every face that comes in out of the street, and most of them twice. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

From there to Moskowitz’s was a fair few blocks. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue, was still serving at this hour, because on Second Avenue nobody goes home until they’ve argued about something over a plate of food. The garlic in the air was thick enough to lean on. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Vogel, the head waiter, was standing by the coats with a menu under his arm, in case anybody wanted one at this hour. Grasso sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in her teeth. She had a pianist’s back, bolt upright, and hands that seemed to be waiting to be counted in. Quill was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. ¶ Stannard had said he was here at eight, and that Grasso was with him at the Bijou at nine. That settled where I was going. Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Vogel had been doing the deciding. ¶ The room had the late quiet of a place that stays open because nobody ever told it to close.

The Broadnax flat was a fair few blocks uptown and east, and I took it at a good clip. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ I went to the Broadnax parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street. The house was old and proud of it, with a carpet on the stairs held down by brass rods, and every rod shone. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Broadnax showed me where the cigarette case had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it went at ten, whoever took it had a key, and the spare key lives in the sugar tin at Rafferty’s. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Rafferty. I went over to her and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. ¶ I asked her who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. She went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Rosenbaum and Zeldin. Nobody else. Nine, Weisglass and Rosenbaum. Nobody else at all. Ten and eleven, nobody but me. The spare key for the Broadnax flat was in its tin at eight. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Zeldin had been in here earlier, when the spare key was there for the taking. Margolis hadn’t been in here while it was there to take. For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Rafferty had nobody. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Zeldin had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Rafferty’s list said otherwise. I wanted to hear what she would say to that. I turned back to her with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody. ¶ “You told me home at ten,” I said. “I wrote it down. Mrs. Rafferty had nobody at Rafferty’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ She looked round to see who was listening, and lowered her voice. “All right. I wasn’t at Rafferty’s. I was at the Automat, meeting Kreuzer, which I promised at home I’d never do again. Ask him. Quietly.” ¶ That was a hole in Zeldin’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, she had been at the Automat at ten, not home. ¶ It turned out Kreuzer had come back in and was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ I didn’t sit in the chair with the short leg. I was unsteady enough.

I waited for a gap in Mosley’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked him to count the night for me, face by face. He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Weisglass and Margolis. Nobody else. Nine, Zeldin and Margolis. Nobody else at all. Ten, Rosenbaum and Margolis. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Margolis. Nobody else. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Lou, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Did you see what was under the coat?” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t ask it its name.” ¶ Mosley had Zeldin here at nine, same as she said. That put Rosenbaum and Margolis here at ten, by his count. Whatever went out of the Broadnax flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Lou. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

Midnight. I was in my office on Mulberry Street, going over the month’s bills by the desk lamp. Flush enough to run the radiator all night, and the radiator, sensing money, actually worked. The cold stayed on its side of the glass. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. My visitor was already diagnosing the room, the stairs and my lack of a secretary before he sat down. ¶ “I’m Patrick Feeney,” he said, sitting down on the edge of the chair. “I was Rufus Tillman’s brother. The police have been and gone, and that’s all they did.” ¶ The dead man was a landlord. At half past eleven, Wehrle, who’d come round to collect a debt, found the body in his own flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ “When was this?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening, the Odessa,” he said. “The usual. Never missed a night.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Ask about Quill,” Feeney said. “He owed Tillman four hundred dollars. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ He counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money and my hat, in that order.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. I went through Tillman’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Wehrle: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted her sister a week before the wedding. Bidwell: a column of payments, every month for years, and his name at the top. Winslow: one line, where he was in 1921, and an address. Quill: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Kowalski’s and the chloral. ¶ Quill was at the Odessa, and I didn’t have a word of his evening yet. ¶ The empty birdcage hung in its corner. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

Mrs. Kowalski’s list had Winslow here at seven. I wanted to hear the other side of it. I said who I was, and he took it about as well as people do. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “I was home at Kowalski’s at seven, with Bidwell. Come eight, I couldn’t settle, so I went to the Odessa for coffee, with Wehrle. Around nine I went to the Automat for coffee and a newspaper. At ten I went home. Nobody was with me at nine or ten.” ¶ Winslow said home at ten. Mrs. Kowalski had nobody here at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. The chloral came from Kowalski’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Quill, Winslow and Bidwell had been at Kowalski’s earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking; Wehrle hadn’t. Winslow had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Kowalski’s list said otherwise. Bidwell was at Kowalski’s at nine; Mrs. Kowalski said so. Quill and Wehrle hadn’t told me where they were at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the cashier at the Odessa who’d been in. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

Moretti’s list had Quill here at seven and nine, so I went over. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was at the Odessa at seven, with Wehrle and Tillman. Then at eight I took a letter round to Kowalski’s, with Bidwell. Come nine, I went to the Odessa to read the late paper over a plate of soup, and stayed the rest of the evening. Wehrle and Tillman were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Quill said the Odessa at ten. The cashier had Wehrle and Bidwell here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Moretti had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ The cashier in the change booth at the Automat would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

I sat at the end of the table with the form, where the light was worst. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ The office radiator always knows when there’s money about. It would be knocking till morning, pleased with itself.

I went over the table. ¶ Brennan didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty bottle with a Weiss’s pharmacy label, the kind that comes off the dispensary shelf. ¶ So the chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Sweeney had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, to get it. ¶ The radiator was still knocking. It was the only thing in the room with anything to say.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Ashby. I asked if the seat was taken. She looked at it for a while before saying it wasn’t. Neat and gray and precise, she wrote everything down, and I had the feeling I’d be written down too before long. ¶ I asked her to tell me her evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. She asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “I was at work, at Weiss’s pharmacy from seven through eight. Reinhardt was there at seven; Prentiss was there at eight. Then I closed up at nine and went to Moskowitz’s for the blue-plate supper, and stayed the rest of the evening. Prentiss and Sweeney were there at nine; Salerno was there at ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Ashby said Moskowitz’s. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ The pen was still going. Whatever I’d done so far, it was in a book now, spelled right.

I found Reinhardt at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “At seven I went to Weiss’s pharmacy to have a prescription made up, with Ashby. Come eight, I went to Moskowitz’s for coffee and pie, with Salerno and Sweeney. Around nine I went to the Eagle club office to write letters, with Salerno. At ten I went to Moskowitz’s for coffee, on my own.” ¶ Reinhardt said Moskowitz’s at ten. Ashby says she was at Moskowitz’s at ten o’clock, with Salerno. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. The chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, so whoever used it had been there first. Reinhardt and Ashby had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking; Salerno hadn’t. Reinhardt had told me Moskowitz’s at ten, and Ashby’s story said otherwise. Salerno was at the Eagle club office at nine and Moskowitz’s at ten; Reinhardt and Ashby said so. Ashby was at Moskowitz’s at ten; Salerno said so. Prentiss hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to know what Prentiss had passed on the way to Moskowitz’s at nine. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

A fair few blocks downtown and east, and I was at Prentiss’s flat. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Prentiss’s flat on Cannon Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner, with a record still on it. ¶ Prentiss answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. ¶ Salerno had passed Prentiss on Hester Street at ten. That settled where I was going. There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

I headed downtown and east for Lindemann’s place, a fair few blocks away. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Lindemann’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street was as high up as the building went. The police had been and gone, and left the place with its lamp lit and its door shut, like a shop on a holiday. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Lindemann was still where they’d found the body, in the chair by the table, as if waiting for something that had come. ¶ Abramowitz was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the chloral already in hand. ¶ I kept my hands in my pockets for the first minute. A room should be looked at before it’s touched.

A good walk uptown and east, and I was at Mrs. Nagy’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Nagy was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Hurwitz, with a bandaged hand, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. Pickering, in a green hat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. ¶ The chloral had come from here. Pickering had found Lindemann. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

I waited at the end of the bar until Mulcahy came down to me, wiping a glass that was already dry. ¶ I asked her to count the night for me, face by face. She counted it off on her fingers, and ran out of fingers before she ran out of night. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Hurwitz, Kreuzer, Pickering and Lindemann. Nobody else. Eight, Hurwitz. Nobody else at all. Nine, Hurwitz, Shapiro and Lindemann. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, somebody in a grey fedora, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. Nobody else.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Mulcahy had Hurwitz, Shapiro and Lindemann at nine and somebody in a grey fedora at ten. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

I sat down near Kreuzer, in a corner nobody else was using. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “I was at Moe’s at seven, with Hurwitz, Pickering and Lindemann. At eight I went to Mrs. Nagy’s for the company, and stayed through nine, with Petrosino and Pickering. Ten o’clock I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning, with Rafferty.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Kreuzer said the print shop. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ It turned out Rafferty was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

Shapiro let me in as far as the kitchen, which in that house was as far as anybody got. I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “At seven I dropped a parcel off at Mrs. Nagy’s, with Petrosino. Eight o’clock I went home to change, on my own. Then at nine I went to Moe’s to settle a bet, with Hurwitz and Lindemann. Come ten, I had a game of gin at home, with Petrosino.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Shapiro said home, here at Shapiro’s flat. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I asked Kaminsky to wait in the hall, and went over the parlor by myself. ¶ He kept out of my way, the way people keep out of the way of a doctor. ¶ The velvet box in the sideboard drawer was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Kaminsky at the Peacock between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Peacock the place to start counting. ¶ The doorkeeper at the Peacock would know who’d been in. ¶ There was a speaking tube by the street door with a brass whistle for every floor, which hasn’t carried a word since 1911, and which every visitor blows into anyway.

Dr. Hirsch watched me come over the way you watch weather. ¶ She was smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window. She had steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you. ¶ “Mrs. Szabo has you here at nine. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ She thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Miss Kahane and Belkin. Come nine, I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door, and stayed the rest of the evening. Nine, I have the cigarette. One. I make it last like a good filling. Amato, Miss Kahane and Mabry were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch said the Peacock at ten. Mrs. Szabo had Amato, Mabry and Miss Marsh here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ There was a stuffed peacock by the bar, molting, with one glass eye; the other was lost in a bet in 1924, and nobody will say who won it. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Dr. Hirsch had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. Amato was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Miss Kahane hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Dr. Hirsch now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. Every question on it had an answer, and every answer had a name and an hour behind it. ¶ At ten Amato was at the Peacock, and Mrs. Szabo said so. Miss Kahane was here, and Pinsky said so. That left one person who had heard about the window, with no true account for ten. ¶ The office stairs had done their bit for the night. They’d brought me the case.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Glick told me twice where everything usually was. I let him. It was his flat, and it was the only thing he could do. ¶ The glass dome on the mantel was empty. The key was back under the mat, and the door hadn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had let themselves in and put the key back after, which is manners of a kind. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the christening supper in the Glick flat at eight. Glick had given me their names. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

Demos was seating a man who would rather have stood. I asked him for everybody he’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because he liked them. ¶ He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat. Tierney the oyster opener was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, nobody else. Nine, Mrs. Ostrow. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody else. No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Tierney, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Under the coat,” I said. “What was it?” ¶ “Something small. If I’d seen more, I’d say more.” ¶ Teitel said Steinmetz’s at ten. The head waiter had Tierney here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Demos had no reason to be the wrong one. Whatever went out of the Glick flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Tierney. ¶ Smoothing his hair with both palms, as if it might have moved: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Teitel and Mrs. Ostrow were at the christening supper and knew the way in; Mrs. Blau wasn’t. Teitel had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Ostrow and Mrs. Blau hadn’t told me where they were at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Tierney, the oyster opener at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Teitel now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. The landlady’s bill was folded under the telephone. I’d see it every time the thing didn’t ring. I decided not to open it until it did. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Somebody has taken a set of silver spoons,” Mrs. Blau said. “It was in the velvet box in the sideboard drawer. It isn’t.” ¶ I offered her the chair and turned the lamp away from her. ¶ “I sat in Sokol’s from eight until ten,” she said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did the spoons go?” ¶ She had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The boy from the delicatessen came up with an order at a quarter past ten and passed somebody on the dark stairs, going down in a hurry.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “I’ll give you a name,” she said. “Dr. Hirsch. She and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ Mrs. Blau said the next part to the desk rather than to me. “Teitel, the pushcart man, owes Doyle money, and he wants it by Saturday. And Mrs. Pomerantz, the wigmaker, has always wanted the spoons, and asked me the price.” ¶ She took a breath, the way people do before the part they’d rather not say. “Glick, the insurance agent, and I haven’t been civil since school.” ¶ She put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with her palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

Sokol’s was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ Sokol’s bakery window had a card in it, lettered by hand, RYE PUMPERNICKEL CHALLAH FRIDAYS, and behind the card the shop was dark except for the glow under the oven doors. Through the back, past the door marked FLOUR, you could hear the radio and the clink of somebody being poured a second one before he’d asked for it. There was a cigar box under the till for lottery slips, which the barman calls receipts. ¶ Sokol was slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Teitel was folding a necktie into a pocket square for a man who hadn’t asked. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. Glick was nursing a small beer and a large worry at the end of the bar. ¶ Mrs. Blau had sat here telling the room about her key. That settled where I was going. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I don’t look up when the door goes. I look up when it doesn’t, because then somebody is standing in it deciding.” ¶ I stood a moment in the door so the room could decide what it thought of me. It didn’t take long.

The card room over Feingold’s garage was round the corner. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ The card room over the garage was down to one table, four players and a pot nobody mentioned. The el had stopped for the night, and the room was quiet enough to hear a card being thought about. The windows were painted black on the inside, so the morning wouldn’t get ideas. There was the outside wooden stair from the garage yard, which creaks on the fourth step, so the room always knows somebody is coming. ¶ Dr. Hirsch was smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window. She had very clean hands with very short nails, and a gold wedding band she wears on a chain round her neck instead of on the hand. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Dr. Hirsch had named Belkin: the card room over Feingold’s garage at ten, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. He was practicing a death scene in the nearest mirror. He had a ring on every finger but one, and a pale band of skin on that one. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, and who he’d seen. ¶ Belkin nodded, as if it were a fair question, and maybe it was. ¶ “My evening! Ah. Sit. As I give everything to my public: from the beginning, with feeling. I was home from eight through nine. At ten I went to the card room over Feingold’s garage to meet Dr. Hirsch. Ten, I am at my best. I have been told so by critics, two of them sober. Eleven o’clock I turned in early, home. I had nobody with me at eight, nine or eleven.” ¶ That put Dr. Hirsch here at ten, and he would swear to it. ¶ The janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ Signing a program nobody asked him to sign: that was the last I saw of him.

I sat on a hard chair in the hall with the form on my knee. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The office telephone never had rung tonight. It hadn’t needed to. The trouble had taken the stairs.

I went over the table. ¶ Mrs. Greco stayed by the door. People in a room with the dead stand where they can leave. ¶ A cup of cocoa gone cold, bitter at the bottom. Beside it a tin with a skull on the label, from the cellar shelf at the flats over Lipsky’s. Somebody made him cocoa. ¶ So the rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, and rat poison takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Russo had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, to get it. ¶ Who was only half of it. The papers at Russo’s place might know the why. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Sokol. ¶ The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. I asked Sokol who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven, I take the last tray out and unlock the door that says flour. One job stops, the other one starts. Seven o’clock, Doyle, Dr. Hirsch and Miss Lowenthal. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Doyle, Kaminsky and Russo. Nobody else at all. Ten, Doyle and Dr. Hirsch. That’s everybody. I counted the glasses twice.” ¶ Doyle hadn’t been at the flats over Lipsky’s while it was there to take. That put Doyle and Dr. Hirsch here at ten, by his count. Mrs. Greco had said nine or ten. Russo was at Sokol’s at nine, alive. ¶ Kaminsky was right here, and I didn’t have his evening yet. ¶ Humming a song from the old country into a glass while he dried it: that was the last I saw of him.

The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. Miss Lowenthal had hair in a tight bun with a pencil through it, which she uses, and a second pencil, which she forgets. ¶ “Sokol has you at Sokol’s at seven. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” Miss Lowenthal thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “My evening was quiet, and I could be quiet about it, but since you ask, here it is. I was at Sokol’s at seven, with Doyle and Dr. Hirsch. Come eight, I went home to change, with Dr. Hirsch. Around nine I went down to the stock room at the Peacock for a quiet drink out of the way. At ten I turned in early, home at the flats over Lipsky’s. I had nobody with me at nine or ten.” ¶ So Sokol’s at seven, with Doyle and Dr. Hirsch, which was what Sokol had. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said home, here at the flats over Lipsky’s. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ Wojcik had been there all night, and would know who came and went. ¶ Drinking tea from a cup with a saucer, always the saucer: that was the last I saw of her.

Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” ¶ Mabry counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Ten, I start hearing tunes in everything: car horns, the el, a woman laughing two streets off. Ten o’clock, Miss Lowenthal and somebody sitting on a crate I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Miss Lowenthal here at ten, by his count. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

I went over the table. ¶ Belkin didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Rafferty’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. Doyle had been drinking with a friend, or with somebody who passed for one. ¶ So the chloral came from Rafferty’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Doyle had been at Rafferty’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I had what there was. A room can’t lie to you, but it can keep quiet.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Amato. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. He had a St. Christopher medal on a chain round his neck and another on the dashboard of his cab, in case one of them is off duty. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “Where to? Ha. Sorry. Habit. Go ahead, ask. I was at Steinmetz’s at seven, with Teitel and Doyle. Eight o’clock I went up to Rafferty’s to pay a call, and stayed through nine. Nine’s dead. Nine’s always dead. You could roll a bowling ball down Delancey at nine. Mrs. Krantz was there at eight; Teitel was there at nine. Then at ten I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee and pie, with Teitel.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Amato said Rafferty’s at nine and Steinmetz’s at ten. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

Miss Nowak had said Teitel was with her here at eight. That was reason enough to ask. He was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. Teitel put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “Sit, sit. My night you can have, and a tie to go with it. I was at Steinmetz’s from seven through eight. Seven, I count the day. It never takes long. Amato and Doyle were there at seven; Miss Nowak and Doyle were there at eight. Nine o’clock I dropped a parcel off at Rafferty’s, with Amato. Then at ten I went to Steinmetz’s for supper, with Amato. Walking over to Steinmetz’s at ten I passed Mrs. Krantz on East Houston Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten and here at seven, with Doyle, which was what Amato had said. One evening that held, at an hour that mattered, where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. East Houston Street was where Doyle lived. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ The undertaker’s cellar was through a coal hole in the Peacock’s back wall, into a long, cold, whitewashed room where the funeral parlor keeps what it keeps. There were trestles, a hand truck and a row of folding chairs for mourners, and the band came through the wall faint and cheerful, like a party nobody down here had been asked to. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. He had a callus on his upper lip from the cornet, which he touches when he’s thinking. ¶ Mabry had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

I headed east for Belkin’s place, a few blocks away. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Rain came down East Houston Street at a slant, and the Excelsior’s awning, green canvas with the name on the scallops, was holding a pond of it that let go every time the wind got underneath. The lobby mat had given up, and the tiles were wet all the way to the foot of the stairs, where the marble begins and the wiping stops. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Belkin was in the chair by the table, head down on folded arms, like somebody asleep over the accounts. He had his greasepaint still on and a program in his coat pocket, signed to himself. ¶ Mrs. Krantz was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I kept my hands in my pockets for the first minute. A room should be looked at before it’s touched.

From there to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s was a couple of blocks. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The bakery cellar under Sokol’s was flour, coal and a row of sourdough crocks with cloths over them, breathing. The ceiling was the oven floor, warm to the hand, and a bulb on a cord lit a stool and an upturned crate with a bottle on it that wasn’t vanilla. There was a bread knife on the bakery counter as long as a man’s forearm, kept sharp enough to slice a roll without waking it. ¶ Mrs. Sobel, with a bandaged hand, was drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth. She had spectacles on a chain, and a face that has seen everybody on Orchard Street at their very first and is not impressed by their since. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had found Belkin. That was reason enough. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

I set off east for the Peacock. It was a couple of blocks. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ With the band gone home, the Peacock looked like what it was: a low cellar with a damp ceiling and the chairs upside down on the tables, smelling of gin and of lilies, the lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s. The steel door was bolted. The slot opened anyway when I knocked, which told me the doorkeeper didn’t go home either. There was an ice pick on the bar beside the block of ice they chip for highballs, with tape wound round the handle for a better grip. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was cracking her knuckles one at a time, in order. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Miss Moskin, in a sailor’s pea coat, was reading Variety for parts uptown. ¶ Belkin had been here earlier in the evening. Mrs. Sobel had said Miss Moskin was with her at her place at nine. That settled where I was going. From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

It was a couple of blocks from there to the flats over Lipsky’s, east, with my collar up. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was the roof door at the top of the stairs, propped open with a brick summer and winter, because nobody has told the brick it’s winter. ¶ Wojcik was eating a sandwich of black bread and onion out of a newspaper. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Mrs. Blau, in a green hat, was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Amato, in a grey fedora, was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. ¶ Miss Moskin had said she was here at seven, eight and nine. Mrs. Szabo’s list had Mrs. Blau at the Peacock at seven, eight and nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I know the tenants by their shoes. Faces, I don’t look at. A face can lie. A shoe has been where it’s been.” ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

Miss Kahane was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. ¶ “Wojcik has you at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven and eight. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ She kept it short. Some people do with everybody. ¶ “My evening. Short version. I worked. Some of us do. At seven I went to the flats over Lipsky’s for a game of pinochle, and stayed through eight, with Mrs. Sobel, Miss Moskin and Amato. Eight’s for leaflets. You fold a thousand, you dream in folds. Around nine I went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. At nine it was just me; Miss Moskin was there at ten.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Kahane said home, here at Miss Kahane’s flat. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ Folding leaflets on the bathtub board, a thousand of them, by lamplight: that was the last I saw of her.

I went over the table. ¶ Rosenbaum watched from the landing with her coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to the Delmonico rooms. Somebody had made Mosley cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from the Delmonico rooms, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Mosley had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ Schilling could tell me his own evening, and he was at the Kit Kat. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

It was a few blocks to Mosley’s place, uptown and east. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Mosley’s place again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Rosenbaum had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Mosley had died here. I wanted another look at the room before I asked anybody anything more. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

The Kit Kat was a fair few blocks uptown and west. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went up the outside stair to the Kit Kat, a speakeasy over a garage. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes. A row of paper lanterns was strung across the room, faded from red to pink by years of smoke. ¶ Donnelly was on a chair tipped back against the door frame, chewing a toothpick down to splinters. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Margolis sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. Schilling was at the bar with his back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. ¶ Mosley had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ Everybody who came in tonight had to get past Donnelly first, and she has the kind of face that remembers who tried. ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

A few blocks uptown and east, and I was at Mosley’s place. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I let myself back into Mosley’s place, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Rosenbaum, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Mosley had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ Tramonti didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty bottle with a Weiss’s pharmacy label, the kind that comes off the dispensary shelf. ¶ So the chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Quill had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, to get it. ¶ Somebody at Hanley’s would have kept count of faces, and that would be the bartender. ¶ The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when the door went. That was all that moved.

From there to Weiss’s pharmacy was a few blocks. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ I went round to Weiss’s pharmacy on Essex Street. The blinds were down, but the big glass jars in the window, one red and one green, were still lit from behind, the way a pharmacy keeps a light on for the sick. A brass scale with a set of little weights stood at one end of the counter, perfectly balanced. ¶ Steinbach was behind her counter in a gray coat, doing the day’s figures by the light of one lamp. Neat and gray and precise, she wrote everything down, and I had the feeling I’d be written down too before long. ¶ The chloral had come from here, and that was worth the walk. Shut or not, nobody comes in at that door without Steinbach looking up from behind the counter to see who it is. ¶ I looked at the brass scale again. Everything weighs something, if you have the little weights.

Quill’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Back at Quill’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Tramonti, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ This was where Quill had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ She sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Carmela Petrosino. I was James Doyle’s landlady. There’s been a murder, and the police are calling it something else.” ¶ Doyle was a pawnbroker. At half past eleven, Grasso, who heard his radio still going and knocked, found the body in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. The police had a look and called it a robbery gone wrong. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ She said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “Shot in the middle of the Atwater Kent Hour, which runs from ten o’clock: the family across the hall turned it up.” ¶ “Every night it was the Orpheum, earlier on,” she said. “Tonight too. The usual.” ¶ “Who had a grudge?” ¶ “Talk to Mosley,” Petrosino said, without having to think about it. “He threw her out of a lease.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Doyle’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Mosley: a notice to quit, from when he threw her out of a lease. Kessler: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Grasso: one line, where she was in 1921, and an address. Mulcahy: a column of payments, every month for years, and his name at the top. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the revolver. ¶ The usher at the Orpheum sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ The calendar went on saying last month. In that room, it might as well.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Grasso. ¶ I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She looked at me for a while first, as if deciding what sort of question it was. ¶ “I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Mulcahy was there at seven; Mosley was there at eight and nine. Ten o’clock I went to the Orpheum to see the new picture, with Kessler.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Grasso said the Orpheum. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ Weisglass would know who’d been in. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at Rafferty’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went back to Rafferty’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. Mosley was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Grasso had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Mosley was with her at her place at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

I got as near to Mosley as manners allowed and said my name. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” She thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was at the Orpheum at seven, alone. Eight o’clock I went home to iron a shirt for the morning, and stayed the rest of the evening. Grasso was there at eight and nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ So here at eight and nine, which was what Grasso had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said home, here at Rafferty’s. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty had been there all night, and would know who came and went. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I asked for the use of a table and got one, and took out the form. It was my name at the bottom, so it had better be my reasons above it. ¶ My head was still keeping time with the clock over the office safe, a little behind and a lot louder.

I went over the floor from wall to wall, looking at the places nobody looks. ¶ Brennan stayed by the door. People in a room with the dead stand where they can leave. ¶ A carving knife lay on the floor by the door. The handle had a mark burnt into it, the mark every knife in the kitchen at Mrs. Nagy’s has so that nobody walks off with one. Somebody had. Carbone had opened the door to somebody and then turned away, which was the mistake. ¶ So the knife came from Mrs. Nagy’s. Carbone died at nine or ten, and whoever used it had been at Mrs. Nagy’s before that, to take it. ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Carbone’s place yet, and papers go on talking after the one who kept them has stopped. ¶ The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when the door went. That was all that moved.

The Velvet Room lay a good walk downtown and west. The cold was still out there doing its rounds. It’s the only thing in this city that works all night for nothing. ¶ I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Ruggiero was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Hauck was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Lathrop sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of her. Abramowitz had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. ¶ Carbone had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Ruggiero looks at everybody twice. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Lathrop had said Abramowitz was with her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. I took the stool next to her. She had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ I mentioned Carbone to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. She looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Carbone closed my business,” she said. “One signature. I watched him do it. He didn’t even sit down.” ¶ That was Abramowitz’s reason, in her own words. Brennan hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating.

From there to the card room was a couple of blocks. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ The card room again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Callahan was shuffling a deck with one hand, not to play, just to keep the hand busy. ¶ Lathrop had said she was here at nine. That settled where I was going. ¶ Whatever had been poured there had set by then. I walked round it.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three. The tenants below had gone home, and the building’s quiet had moved in and made itself comfortable. Through the window the sky had gone perfectly clear. I hadn’t looked up in a while. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. A woman came in, coat buttoned against the cold, and asked straight off what it would cost. I liked her. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Maureen Corrigan. Roscoe Ashby’s business partner, or I was till tonight, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Ashby was a bail bondsman. Cheatham, who’d come up for the Thursday card game, found the body in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair. She took it, and held her hat on her knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” she said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was the Orpheum,” she said. “The usual. You could have set a clock by it.” ¶ “Who had a grudge?” ¶ “There’s Quill,” she said. “I don’t like gossip, but He had a file on him. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ Corrigan put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. The papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box people keep for the things they’d rather not file. ¶ There was a page on everybody with a grudge, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. They’d been kept square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Tillman: a notice to quit, from when he threw him out of a lease. Cheatham: the order that closed his business, with his signature on it. Hurwitz: a court transcript, his own testimony against his brother. Quill: a file he’d kept on him, thick enough to matter. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Cheatham’s surgery and the chloral. ¶ I didn’t touch the empty birdcage. Some things in a room are only there to be sad.

Cheatham’s surgery was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ Back at Cheatham’s surgery, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Mulcahy was at the desk with his hat already on, as if going home were only a matter of finishing one more page. ¶ The chloral had come from here. That settled where I was going. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating.

Tillman’s flat was a fair few blocks uptown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ Tillman’s flat on Pitt Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner, with a record still on it. ¶ Tillman was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. He was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until he needed one, and then only the one. ¶ Quill had passed Tillman on Grand Street at ten. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Quill had passed Tillman on Grand Street at ten. I knew a little of his evening and nothing of his reasons, and I wanted both. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I mentioned Ashby to Tillman and let the quiet do some of the asking. Tillman looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Ashby threw me out of a lease,” he said. “I did everything right. It didn’t matter. It never does, with a man like that.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Corrigan hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ I passed the gramophone and left it alone. Some nights don’t need music.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. I’d paid the landlady on my way up, and she’d counted it on the landing in front of me. The stairs felt shorter for it. The office looked the same as always, which was its own kind of relief. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ He sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Albrecht Wehrle. I was Carmine Salerno’s brother-in-law. There’s been a murder, and the police are calling it something else.” ¶ The dead man was a buildings inspector, found dead in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street at half past eleven by Lathrop, who heard his radio still going and knocked. The police put it down as a robbery gone wrong. ¶ “When did it happen?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: eight or nine o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was Hanley’s,” he said. “The usual. You could have set a clock by it.” ¶ “Who’d have wanted that?” ¶ “Ask about Havemeyer,” Wehrle said. “He owed Salerno four hundred dollars. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money. By the end of the week it would belong to my landlady, but for tonight the two of us were getting along fine.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. Salerno kept the papers in a box file, and I sat down with it under the lamp. ¶ The papers held a page on everybody with a grudge, kept like a doctor’s files, one grudge to a page and every page full. ¶ Hanrahan: the order that closed her business, with his signature on it. Lathrop: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted his sister a week before the wedding. Havemeyer: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. Doyle: a file he’d kept on him, thick enough to matter. Carbone: a column of payments, every month for years, and her name at the top. ¶ A reason is the easy half. Everybody in Salerno’s box had one. ¶ I didn’t touch the empty birdcage. Some things in a room are only there to be sad.

Hanrahan was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from her yet. That was one thing. How Hanrahan felt about the whole business was another, and I wanted to hear it. ¶ I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ I asked her about Salerno. Her mouth went flat. She didn’t like the question, and didn’t mind my knowing it. ¶ “Salerno closed my business,” she said. “I still carry the key. I don’t know why. There’s nothing left for it to open.” ¶ That was her reason, in her own words. Wehrle hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I walked downtown and west to the Automat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went into the Automat on Delancey Street, open all night. It was a long bright room of little glass doors, each with a sandwich or a slice of pie behind it, and a nickel would open any one of them. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Carbone, with a bandaged hand, was in the corner with a cup of coffee, holding it in both hands for the warmth. ¶ Hanrahan had said Carbone was with her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

Hanrahan had said Carbone was with her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. I waited until she had finished what she was doing, which took longer than it needed to. ¶ I mentioned Salerno to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. She took a moment over it, then answered at an even pace. ¶ “Salerno had been squeezing me for years,” she said. “I could tell you the day it started. I couldn’t have told you when it would stop.” ¶ That was Carbone’s reason, in her own words. Wehrle hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ A reason tells you who might have wanted to. It doesn’t tell you who did.

I sat down at the kitchen table with the form, under the one good light. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The office stairs would still be a little shorter when I climbed them next. Paid rent does that to a building.

I went over the table. ¶ Miss Kahane watched from the landing with her coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A cup of cocoa gone cold, bitter at the bottom. Beside it a tin with a skull on the label, from the cellar shelf at the flats over Lipsky’s. Somebody made him cocoa. ¶ So the rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, and rat poison takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Kaminsky had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, to get it. ¶ The papers were still at Kaminsky’s place, and nobody had read them yet but the one who wrote them. ¶ There was a speaking tube by the street door with a brass whistle for every floor, which hasn’t carried a word since 1911, and which every visitor blows into anyway.

Kaminsky’s place was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Kaminsky’s place again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Miss Kahane had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Kaminsky had died here. I wanted another look at the room before I asked anybody anything more. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

The Peacock was a couple of blocks west. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ With the band gone home, the Peacock looked like what it was: a low cellar with a damp ceiling and the chairs upside down on the tables, smelling of gin and of lilies, the lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s. The steel door was bolted. The slot opened anyway when I knocked, which told me the doorkeeper didn’t go home either. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was cracking her knuckles one at a time, in order. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Russo was sitting with his back to the wall. Margolis was listening to an engine nobody else could hear. ¶ Kaminsky had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

Kaminsky’s place was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I let myself back into Kaminsky’s place, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Miss Kahane, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Kaminsky had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ Mrs. Krantz didn’t come in. I didn’t ask her to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty brown bottle with a surgery label on it: Dr. Hirsch’s surgery. ¶ So the chloral came from Dr. Hirsch’s surgery, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Belkin had been at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery earlier, to get it. ¶ Somebody at Steinmetz’s would have kept count of faces, and that would be the head waiter. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

From there to Dr. Hirsch’s surgery was a good walk. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ The bank’s brass doors were shining wet, and up the side stair the dentist’s waiting room had an umbrella stand full of umbrellas nobody came back for: people with toothaches forget everything, and people without them don’t come back. There was a cylinder of laughing gas on a trolley, with a rubber mask that has seen a great many faces at their worst. ¶ Miss Gutman was writing appointment cards in her best hand. Teeth so perfect people assume the doctor did them; she was born with them, and she’ll tell you. ¶ The chloral had come from here, and that was worth the walk. From her post Miss Gutman could see the waiting room and the stairs up from the street. “I can tell a patient from a visitor on the stairs. A patient comes up slow and holds his jaw. A visitor comes up quick and holds his hat.” ¶ There was a stack of magazines in the waiting room old enough that the patients read them as history.

Belkin’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Back at Belkin’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Mrs. Krantz, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ This was where Belkin had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ She sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Bertha Krantz. I was Francis Doyle’s old sweetheart. There’s been a murder, and the police are calling it something else.” ¶ The dead man was the alderman’s clerk. At half past eleven, Miss Nowak, who’d come to settle a bet, found the body in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ Mrs. Krantz said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “The chop house sent up his supper at ten o’clock, and the coroner found chloral in it; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “Every night it was Steinmetz’s, earlier on,” she said. “Tonight too. The usual.” ¶ “Who had a grudge?” ¶ “Teitel made a scene in the street on Monday, in front of the fruit man,” Mrs. Krantz said. “I’d start there. He owed Doyle money and couldn’t pay it.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Doyle’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Miss Nowak: a complaint against Miss Kahane, with her name pencilled at the bottom. Amato: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mabry: an IOU from his friend, with his name pencilled beside it. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the chloral. ¶ The head waiter at Steinmetz’s sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Nowak. She was counting out change for a horse she likes. She was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. She took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Mabry was there at seven and eight; Amato was there at nine. Eight’s when I feel lucky. I don’t know why. It’s cost me a fortune. Come ten, I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Teitel.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Nowak said Steinmetz’s. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ Demos would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ I wrote it down hour by hour, and underlined nothing.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at Rafferty’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went back to Rafferty’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open. Mabry was eating pie at four in the morning. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Mabry was with her at her place at seven. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing: that was the last I saw of her.

There was a pot of tea stewing on the back of the stove at all hours, offered to everybody, and always too strong to refuse politely. Mabry had a pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been. ¶ I asked Mabry for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “My night? I’ll play it straight, no improvising. Takes the fun out, but you asked. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through eight, with Miss Nowak. Seven, I warm up my lip. Wherever I am, the lip comes too. Come nine, I went to Steinmetz’s to read the late paper over a plate of soup, with Teitel and Doyle. Around ten I went home to bed, by myself.” ¶ So here at seven and eight, which was what Miss Nowak had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said home, here at Rafferty’s. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ There was Parnell, a ginger cat, asleep on a different stair every time anybody comes in, as if he were keeping count for her.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. A man came in exactly on the hour, as if he’d booked it, and waited for me to catch up. ¶ “Vincent Amato,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Leo Kaminsky’s friend, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ Kaminsky was the prizefighter. Dr. Hirsch, who heard his radio still going and knocked, found the body in his own flat in the Belvedere on Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The police called it a robbery gone wrong and went home. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair.
