He took it, and held his hat on his knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was the Lyric,” he said. “The usual. You could have set a clock by it.” ¶ “Who’d want it badly enough to see to it?” ¶ “There was a letter from Lieb in the desk,” he said. “He knew things about him only an old friend would. Start with him.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Amato said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I put the money in my wallet, where it looked lonely and slightly surprised.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Kaminsky’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Lieb: a sealed envelope with his name on it. Dr. Hirsch: a letter from her asking for her money, never answered. Miss Nowak: letters from her friend, and her name on the last of them. Miss Kahane: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the revolver. ¶ Somebody at the Lyric would have kept count of faces, and that would be the usher. ¶ There was a speaking tube by the street door with a brass whistle for every floor, which hasn’t carried a word since 1911, and which every visitor blows into anyway.

Dr. Hirsch had found Kaminsky. A where without a why is half an answer, and I wanted the other half from her. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. She had steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you. ¶ I asked her about Kaminsky. “You’re probing, and I don’t see why I should sit still for it.” ¶ “The Kaminsky boy owes me for two front teeth I put back after a fight he says he won.” ¶ That was Dr. Hirsch’s reason, in her own words. Amato hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. ¶ Reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead: that was the last I saw of her.

I went round the corner to Rafferty’s. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ Back at Rafferty’s, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open. Miss Nowak was painting her nails a red her landlady disapproves of. ¶ Miss Kahane had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Miss Nowak was with her here at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Counting the umbrellas on their hooks: that was the last I saw of her.

Mrs. Rafferty was darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing. ¶ I asked her for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. She didn’t look at the room to answer. She didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven, I take my chair and the mending, and the house knows I’m on. Seven o’clock, Miss Kahane and Miss Nowak. Nobody else. Eight, Lieb and Miss Kahane. Nobody else at all. Nine, Miss Kahane and Miss Nowak. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The revolver in the hall-stand drawer was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Lieb, Miss Kahane and Miss Nowak had been here earlier, when the revolver was there for the taking. Dr. Hirsch hadn’t been here while it was there to take. Mrs. Rafferty had Miss Kahane here at seven, same as she said. That put Miss Nowak here at nine, by her count. ¶ There was Parnell, a ginger cat, asleep on a different stair every time anybody comes in, as if he were keeping count for her.

It was a few blocks from there to Doyle’s place, east, with my collar up. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ After midnight East Houston Street was trolley wires and wet light, and the Excelsior’s front door was the only one on the block with a brass kick plate polished by tenants’ shoes instead of a janitor. Inside, the stairs went up into the dark from a lobby lamp nobody owns, past landings where every door had its tenant’s name in a little brass frame. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle lay on the floor on one side, where the fall had left the body, with the knees drawn up a little. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Teitel was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, uptown and west to Rafferty’s, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was the mending basket, set square across the top of the first flight, so that coming up the stairs means asking it to move. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was pouring tea nobody asked for. She had reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again. ¶ The revolver had come from here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “Every lodger I have climbs those stairs his own way, and I know them all by it: two at a time, or stopping on the fourth for breath, or in his stocking feet thinking I’m asleep.” ¶ The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Nowak. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Mrs. Pomerantz was there at seven; Mrs. Krantz was there at eight; Miss Kahane was there at nine. Around ten I went to Steinmetz’s to read the late paper over a plate of soup, with Miss Kahane.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Miss Nowak said home at nine and Steinmetz’s at ten. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

Getting to Steinmetz’s meant a couple of blocks west. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I let myself back into Steinmetz’s, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Demos was smoothing his hair with both palms, as if it might have moved. Mrs. Pomerantz was looking at a stranger’s hair as if pricing it. Miss Nowak sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Miss Kahane had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at ten, and that Mrs. Pomerantz was with her at her place at seven. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Writing covers in the book at his stand: that was the last I saw of him.

It was no distance to Doyle’s place: round the corner, and there it was. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ I went back to Doyle’s place, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Teitel, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ This was where Doyle had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

Doyle’s place lay a few blocks east. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ After midnight East Houston Street was trolley wires and wet light, and the Excelsior’s front door was the only one on the block with a brass kick plate polished by tenants’ shoes instead of a janitor. Inside, the stairs went up into the dark from a lobby lamp nobody owns, past landings where every door had its tenant’s name in a little brass frame. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle was in the chair with the head to one side, like somebody dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it happened at eight or nine, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

It was no distance to the flats over Lipsky’s: round the corner, and there it was. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ The tenement over Lipsky’s was dark from the stoop to the roof, except one kitchen on the third floor where somebody was ironing a shirt for the morning. The shop window below had a card in it, EVERYTHING MUST GO, which had been saying so since the war. There was a row of tin mailboxes in the hall, with the names in five different hands and two crossed out. ¶ Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. Mrs. Krantz, in a fur collar, was counting bills with a rubber thumb. Teitel, in a sailor’s pea coat, was haggling with a customer who had already paid. ¶ The rat poison had come from here. Teitel had found Doyle, and that was worth the walk. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I know the tenants by their shoes. Faces, I don’t look at. A face can lie. A shoe has been where it’s been.” ¶ The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown to Doyle’s place, a few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ Back at Doyle’s place, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ My client, Dr. Hirsch, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in her hand. ¶ This was where Doyle had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

From there to Russo’s flat was a couple of blocks. East Houston Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I went back to Russo’s flat, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Russo, with a bandaged hand, was sitting with his back to the wall. ¶ Teitel had said Russo was with him at his place at seven. That was reason enough. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

A few blocks downtown, and I was at Doyle’s place. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Back at Doyle’s place. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Dr. Hirsch let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Doyle had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

I went over Grasso’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Grasso told me twice where everything usually was. I let him. It was his flat, and it was the only thing he could do. ¶ The hook by the window where the cage hung was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Grasso at the chop house between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the chop house the place to start counting. ¶ Somebody at the chop house would have kept count of faces, and that would be the head waiter. ¶ The aspidistra in the corner shone, leaf by leaf. It was the best-kept thing in the room, and it knew it.

Lathrop had a cup he’d stopped drinking and a newspaper he’d stopped reading, and was keeping both for company. ¶ I sat down across from him with a cup of coffee for company. ¶ “Fairbanks has you here at nine. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” ¶ He went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “At eight I dropped a parcel off at Mrs. Nagy’s, with Ainsworth. Around nine I went to the chop house for a glass of tea, and stayed the rest of the evening. Alfano, Lefkowitz and Dettweiler were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Lathrop said the chop house at ten. Fairbanks had Alfano, Dettweiler and Lou here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Lathrop had told me the chop house at ten, and Fairbanks’s list said otherwise. Alfano was at the chop house at ten; Fairbanks said so. Lefkowitz hadn’t told me where he was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the chop house at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Lathrop now. Or I could find out first from the landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s who’d been in. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

I found a chair at Mrs. Nagy’s and sat down with the form. There was nothing on it I couldn’t fill in. ¶ At ten Alfano was at the chop house, and Fairbanks said so. Lefkowitz was here, and Mrs. Nagy said so. That left one person who had heard about the window, with no true account for ten. ¶ The coffee on my desk would have gone the rest of the way cold by now. I’d finish it anyway. I’d started it, and I’m a professional.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Weisglass stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The basket by the stove was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Weisglass at the Blue Lantern between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Blue Lantern the place to start counting. ¶ Somebody at the Blue Lantern would have kept count of faces, and that would be the doorkeeper. ¶ Bless This House, said the sampler. It hadn’t said anything about the people coming into it.

Hargrove’s list had Dettweiler here at eight. That was reason enough to ask. I sat down one stool away from her, which gave her room to decide about me. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ She thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I was at the Blue Lantern at eight, with Salerno. Around nine I went to the chop house to read the late paper over a plate of soup, with Petrosino. At ten I went to the Blue Lantern, because a friend was on the door, by myself.” ¶ Dettweiler said the Blue Lantern at ten. Hargrove had Benny here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Dettweiler and Salerno were at the Blue Lantern while Weisglass told the room; Grasso wasn’t. Dettweiler had told me the Blue Lantern at ten, and Hargrove’s list said otherwise. Grasso and Salerno hadn’t told me where they were at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at the Blue Lantern at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Dettweiler now. Or I could find out first from the head waiter at the chop house who’d been in. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

I found a chair at the chop house and sat down with the form. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ My ribs had let me breathe through all of it, if shallow. I thanked them and didn’t push my luck.

I went over Prentiss’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Prentiss stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The basket by the stove was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Prentiss at Moskowitz’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Moskowitz’s the place to start counting. ¶ The head waiter at Moskowitz’s sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ The aspidistra in the corner hadn’t moved, which is the great thing about aspidistras.

Hochstetter’s list had Winslow here at eight. That was reason enough to ask. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” Winslow put down what she was holding and gave me her attention. ¶ “I was at Moskowitz’s at eight, with Renfro. Then at nine I went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. Moretti was there at nine and ten; at eleven it was just me.” ¶ So here at eight, with Renfro, which was what Hochstetter had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For eleven, the hour that mattered, she said home at Mrs. Nagy’s. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ Carbone hadn’t told me his evening yet, and he was at the Automat. ¶ Nobody counted anybody in. I nearly counted them in myself, out loud, just to get things started.

Carbone had told me Moskowitz’s at eleven, and Hochstetter’s list said otherwise. That wanted putting to him before it went any further. He saw the notebook in my hand and knew what it meant before I opened my mouth. ¶ I put it to him straight. “You said Moskowitz’s at eleven. Hochstetter had Moretti, Renfro and Pardo at Moskowitz’s at eleven o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ He closed his eyes for a second, like somebody hearing a bill read out that he’d known was coming. “All right. I wasn’t at Moskowitz’s. I was at the Automat, with Bellucci. Ask him, and I’d thank you not to spread it.” ¶ That was a hole in Carbone’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, he had been at the Automat at eleven, not at Moskowitz’s. ¶ It turned out Bellucci was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The tin sign was still promising relief. It had been promising it for years.

I asked Mrs. Nagy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Carbone and Moretti. Nobody else. Nine and ten, Winslow and Moretti. Nobody else at all. Eleven, nobody but me.” ¶ Winslow said home at eleven. The landlady had nobody here at eleven o’clock. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. Mrs. Nagy had Carbone here at eight, same as he said. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Lefkowitz’s place was a few blocks east, and I took it at a good clip. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went up to Lefkowitz’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. Two rooms, a front and a back, with the police gone and the clock on the shelf still ticking, as if nobody had told it. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Lefkowitz was in the chair by the table, head down on folded arms, like somebody asleep over the accounts. ¶ Kavanagh, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a couple of blocks from there to Moskowitz’s, uptown and west, with my collar up. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Corrigan was going from table to table with a cloth over his arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Abramowitz sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. Alfano sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Winslow was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. ¶ A head waiter shows everybody to a table, so Corrigan would know who had come in tonight and where they’d been put. ¶ I took a seat where I could see the door, which is the only habit of mine that ever paid.

From there to the Delmonico rooms were a fair few blocks. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Lindemann had the parlor door open and the parlor lamp on, so that nothing in the hall could happen without an audience. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Sirkin was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ Abramowitz had said she was here at seven. Corrigan’s list had Sirkin at Moskowitz’s at seven, and that was worth the walk. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

The print shop was a good walk uptown and west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went in at the print shop on Centre Street, which runs a night shift. The presses were running with a noise like a train going over a long bridge, and everything in the room smelled of ink and hot oil. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Reinhardt was at her desk, going down a sheet of names with a ruler, line by line. ¶ Reinhardt runs the night shift, and knows who came on, who went off, and who said they’d only be a minute. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

Renfro’s place was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ I climbed to Renfro’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street. The drugstore below was dark, and the only sound in the building was the stair under my feet. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Renfro was still where they’d found the body, in the chair by the table, as if waiting for something that had come. ¶ Feeney let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

I set off east for the chop house. It was a couple of blocks. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Donnelly stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Hurwitz had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. Sirkin was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Crowninshield sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. ¶ A head waiter seats everybody who comes in, which means a head waiter knows where everybody sat. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Donnelly’s list had Sirkin here at seven and ten. I wanted the rest of it in his own words. ¶ I got as near to Sirkin as manners allowed and said my name. He had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ He minded a little, then decided it was cheaper not to. ¶ “I was at the chop house at seven, with Crowninshield. Around eight I went to Mrs. Nagy’s for a game of pinochle, and stayed through nine. Bellucci was there at eight; Crowninshield was there at nine. At ten I went to the chop house to read the late paper over a plate of soup, with Crowninshield.” ¶ So here at ten and seven, with Crowninshield, which was what Donnelly had. One evening that held, at an hour that mattered, where I could check it. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating.

I asked Hanrahan for a minute, and he gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ I asked Hanrahan who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Hurwitz. Nobody else. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Hurwitz here at ten, by his count. ¶ Bellucci had walked from Mrs. Nagy’s to the chop house at nine. I wanted to know what he’d passed on the way. ¶ The toes were still ready to be somewhere else. So were mine, but mine were further from the door.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. I put down what I had, and what I had would have to stand up by itself. ¶ The rent envelope on my desk could stop worrying. For once I had something to put in it.

I got down and went over the floor with a flashlight, board by board. ¶ Brauer stayed by the door. People in a room with the dead stand where they can leave. ¶ A carving knife lay on the floor by the door. The handle had a mark burnt into it, the mark every knife in the kitchen at Mrs. Nagy’s has so that nobody walks off with one. Somebody had. Bellucci had opened the door to somebody and then turned away, which was the mistake. ¶ So the knife came from Mrs. Nagy’s. Bellucci died at nine or ten, and whoever used it had been at Mrs. Nagy’s before that, to take it. ¶ The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when the door went. That was all that moved.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Doyle. ¶ I got as near to him as manners allowed and said my name. I asked him to walk me through his night, every stop of it. ¶ He nodded, as if it were a fair question, and maybe it was. ¶ “I was home at Mrs. Nagy’s from seven through nine. Rosenbaum and Prentiss were there at seven; Schilling and Prentiss were there at eight and nine. Around ten I went to the Palace to sit through the double bill, with Lathrop.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Doyle said home at nine and the Palace at ten. That was his word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ It turned out Lathrop was three rows back with her hat over her eyes. ¶ Nobody had fixed the chair with the short leg. In a room like that, a folded matchbook under the leg counts as a carpenter.

I waited for a gap in Ellery’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ He didn’t look at the room to answer. He didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Vitale and Schilling. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Vitale and Bellucci. Nobody else at all. Ten, somebody in a camel coat, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ I wrote down what Ellery had at nine and ten, the hours that mattered: Vitale and Bellucci at nine and somebody in a camel coat at ten. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

I asked Mrs. Nagy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ I asked her who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Doyle, Rosenbaum and Prentiss. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Doyle, Schilling and Prentiss. Nobody else at all. Ten, Vitale and Prentiss. Nobody else, that hour. The carving knife in my kitchen drawer was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Nagy had Vitale and Prentiss. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three. The coffee I’d made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor knocked once, came in, and sat down like somebody who’d been rehearsing it on the stairs. ¶ “Mimi’s gone,” Glick said. “My Persian. She sleeps on the window seat, and she isn’t there.” ¶ “I had people in at eight for the burial society’s meeting,” he said. “Mabry, Mrs. Ostrow and Mrs. Krantz. Nobody else.” ¶ “The parlor window onto the fire escape won’t latch,” he said. “I showed everybody at the table. I laughed about it.” He wasn’t laughing now. ¶ “And when did Mimi go?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “The dog next door went off at ten o’clock, the way it does when somebody’s on the stairs.” ¶ “Anybody you can think of who’d want Mimi?” ¶ “Look at Mabry,” he said. “He picked Mimi up and asked what she cost at the meeting. Who does that? And he owes Mrs. Blau money, and she isn’t a patient woman.” ¶ Then, almost as an afterthought: “Mrs. Ostrow, the matchmaker, has always wanted Mimi, and asked me the price. And Mrs. Krantz, the rent collector, and I haven’t been civil since school.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Glick said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where Mimi is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

The Lyric was a few blocks west, and I took it at a good clip. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There was the usher’s seating chart on a clipboard, every seat sold a pencil cross. ¶ Pinsky was waxing the points of his mustache with a licked finger. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. Mrs. Ostrow was looking at a stranger as if measuring him for a wife. ¶ Glick had pointed me at Mabry, who picked Mimi up and asked what she cost at the meeting. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “Nobody comes in late past me. They wait at the doors for the end of the scene like everybody else, and while they wait, I look at them.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Steinmetz’s was a fair few blocks downtown. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ Demos was smoothing his hair with both palms, as if it might have moved. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. Margolis was wiping his hands on a rag that made them dirtier. ¶ Mabry had said he was here at nine, with Margolis. That settled where I was going. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.” ¶ I bought a coffee to look like I belonged. It cost a nickel, and I got about a nickel’s worth.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. A man stood in the doorway, cap on, deciding if I was worth coming in for. Narrowly. ¶ “Fritz’s gone,” Doyle said. “My dachshund. He sleeps in his basket by the stove, and he isn’t there.” ¶ I got up and offered him the chair, and he sat down in it carefully, the way people sit in chairs they don’t trust. ¶ “I sat in Sokol’s from eight until ten,” he said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The man below heard the door go just after the ten o’clock el went by; he sets his watch by it.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “Talk to Russo,” he said, without having to think about it. “He and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ Then, smaller: “Mrs. Krantz, the rent collector, says Fritz was promised to her, back in my courting days. And Teitel, the pushcart man, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” Doyle said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

It was a couple of blocks to Sokol’s, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. I thought of the couple under the umbrella. They’d have got somewhere by now, or given up and found a doorway. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was the back booth, behind a wall of flour sacks, where the bookmaker sits with a pencil and a cup of coffee he never finishes. ¶ Sokol was looking in on the ovens through the door marked FLOUR. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. ¶ Doyle had sat here telling the room about his parlor window. That was reason enough. From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I don’t look up when the door goes. I look up when it doesn’t, because then somebody is standing in it deciding.” ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks downtown and east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ Rain had driven the night’s last customers out of Steinmetz’s and the morning’s first ones hadn’t come. The chop house’s awning was sagging with a lake of water, which a waiter was poking up from underneath with a broom handle to watch it go over the edge in one piece, and then doing it again. There was a rack of bone-handled steak knives by the kitchen door, counted out at noon and counted back at closing, more or less. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Mrs. Krantz was writing in a rent book with a fountain pen. Kaminsky was eating a steak he couldn’t afford, slowly, to make it last. ¶ Teitel had said he was here at nine, and that Mrs. Krantz was with him at Sokol’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Midnight. I was in my office on Mulberry Street, going over the month’s bills by the desk lamp. I hadn’t slept since the night before the night before. The clock over the door had stopped pretending that mattered to it. I let it keep its own count. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor hung up his own coat and sat like a man who’d waited in better rooms and billed for it. ¶ “Somebody has taken my Pomeranian,” Glick said. “Duchess. Gone from her cushion by the radiator, just like that.” ¶ “I had people in at eight,” he said, “for the burial society’s meeting. Belkin, Mrs. Krantz and Miss Nowak. Nobody else came.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “And when did Duchess go?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “St. Teresa’s was striking eleven when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want to take her?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Miss Nowak,” he said. “She owes Fishel money, and he wants it by Saturday.” ¶ He looked at the window, then back at me. “Mrs. Krantz, the rent collector, and I haven’t been civil since school. And Mrs. Sobel, the midwife, has always wanted Duchess, and asked me the price.” ¶ He counted them off on his fingers without meaning to. “Belkin, the leading man, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday.” ¶ Glick counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I put the money in my wallet, where it looked lonely and slightly surprised.

I headed west for Rafferty’s, a couple of blocks away. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was a row of umbrella hooks in the hall, each with a lodger’s name inked over it, and one with no name that nobody will explain. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open. She had a ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes. Miss Nowak was writing a letter home to Scranton. ¶ Glick had pointed me at Miss Nowak, who asked twice whether Duchess had papers at the meeting, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “Every lodger I have climbs those stairs his own way, and I know them all by it: two at a time, or stopping on the fourth for breath, or in his stocking feet thinking I’m asleep.” ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eleven’s the hour for the last good tune. After that everybody’s playing for tips. Eleven o’clock, Miss Nowak and somebody sitting on a crate I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before eleven. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ Miss Nowak said home at eleven. Mabry had her here at eleven o’clock. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ The bulb on its cord gave the place all the light it was going to get, which wasn’t much. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at eleven o’clock. Mrs. Krantz, Belkin and Miss Nowak were at the meeting and knew the way in; Mrs. Sobel wasn’t. Miss Nowak had told me home at eleven, and Mabry’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Krantz, Mrs. Sobel and Belkin hadn’t told me where they were at eleven, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out what Belkin had to say for himself. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Demos was holding a fork up to the light. I asked him who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. ¶ He looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat. Tierney the oyster opener was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, nobody else. Nine, Belkin. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody else. Eleven, Mrs. Krantz and Mrs. Sobel. No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so.” ¶ Belkin said Steinmetz’s at eleven. The head waiter had Mrs. Krantz, Mrs. Sobel and Tierney here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Demos had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ Writing covers in the book at his stand: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. The retainer was still folded in my breast pocket. I’d checked for it twice on the walk up, which wasn’t like me. I put it in the drawer, where it would keep its shape better than I would. ¶ The street door went downstairs, and somebody started up, taking the stairs slowly, like somebody not sure they were the right stairs. A woman came in talking, and kept it up through the whole business of getting seated: her gloves, her appointment book, and finally the reason for coming. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Bertha Krantz. Carmine Russo’s neighbor, or I was till tonight, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Russo was the card-room keeper. Kaminsky, who’d come round to collect a debt, found the body in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ I offered Mrs. Krantz the chair. She looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” she said. “The coroner says rat poison in a drink, taken at nine or ten o’clock; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was the Lyric,” she said. “The usual. You could have set a clock by it.” ¶ “Who had a grudge?” ¶ “Amato made a scene in the street on Monday, in front of the fruit man,” she said. “I’d start there. He knew things about him only an old friend would.” ¶ “The police have their answer,” Mrs. Krantz said, and put fifty dollars on my desk. “I want the right one.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. I went through the papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Dr. Hirsch: a tally of what she owed him, added up twice. Doyle: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Amato: a sealed envelope with his name on it. Kaminsky: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the rat poison, and that was at the flats over Lipsky’s. ¶ The usher at the Lyric sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ I left it as I found it, give or take my fingerprints.

From there to the kitchen at Steinmetz’s was a fair few blocks. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ Past the swinging door the kitchen at Steinmetz’s was a long, low, hot room of black ranges and copper pans, with steam hanging under the ceiling and a floor mopped so often it had gone soft. A row of chops waited on a marble slab under a cloth like patients, and a cleaver stood up in the block by the door where somebody had left it. There was a rack of bone-handled steak knives by the kitchen door, counted out at noon and counted back at closing, more or less. ¶ Kaminsky was eating a raw egg out of the shell, for the strength. He had a nose that has been broken twice, once in each direction, so that it has come out more or less straight. ¶ Pinsky’s list had Kaminsky at the Lyric at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

Kaminsky had named Miss Nowak: the kitchen at Steinmetz’s at ten, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. She was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. ¶ I asked her for her evening, all of it, and kept the other story in my pocket. ¶ Miss Nowak thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. I was home from seven through nine, alone. Seven, I still hear the switchboard in my ears. It takes till eight to stop. Then at ten I went to the kitchen at Steinmetz’s to meet Kaminsky.” ¶ That put Kaminsky here at ten, on her word. ¶ Somebody at the flats over Lipsky’s would have kept count of faces, and that would be the janitor. ¶ Counting out change for a horse she likes: that was the last I saw of her.

Wojcik’s list had Amato here at eight and nine. I wanted the rest of it in his own words. ¶ The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. He was a stocky man in a leather jacket and a chauffeur’s cap pushed back, moving a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other to show he’s thinking. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter. I was at the Lyric at seven, with Dr. Hirsch, Doyle and Russo. Come eight, I went home, and stayed the rest of the evening. Dr. Hirsch was there at eight and nine; at ten it was just me. Ten, the shows let out and everybody wants Brooklyn. Nobody wants Brooklyn at any other hour.” ¶ Amato said home at ten. Wojcik had nobody here at ten o’clock. Two stories about him at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ Eating a sandwich at the kitchen window with one eye on his cab in the street: that was the last I saw of him.

I walked east to Doyle’s place. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ After midnight East Houston Street was trolley wires and wet light, and the Excelsior’s front door was the only one on the block with a brass kick plate polished by tenants’ shoes instead of a janitor. Inside, the stairs went up into the dark from a lobby lamp nobody owns, past landings where every door had its tenant’s name in a little brass frame. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle was on the floor between the table and the door. Nobody had put a sheet over the body yet, or closed the eyes. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Mrs. Krantz let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

I set off uptown for Miss Kahane’s flat. It was a couple of blocks. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ By that hour the Belvedere had gone dark from the pickle store to the roof, every flat but one, where a kitchen light was on and a kettle was beginning to think about it. The stairs creaked under nobody at all, the way old stairs do at night, settling the day’s accounts. There was the street door’s lock, broken since Purim, and a loop of string over a nail that does the lock’s work for it. ¶ Miss Kahane was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. She had a cardboard suitcase of leaflets she carries everywhere, held shut with a belt. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had pointed me at Miss Kahane. That was reason enough. Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

I sat down where Teitel could see me, and didn’t hurry. He had a white beard trimmed square, and fingerless gloves from which he can produce change faster than you can see it. ¶ “Mr. Teitel. I’d like your evening, if you can spare it. Where were you, and who was with you?” He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. I was at the Peacock at seven, with Belkin. At eight I went to Rafferty’s to collect a debt, with Miss Nowak. Nine o’clock I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play. Then at ten I went to the Peacock to see who was about. At nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, he said the card room over Feingold’s garage at nine and the Peacock at ten. It went in the notebook in his own words. ¶ Folding a necktie into a pocket square for a man who hadn’t asked: that was the last I saw of him.

Mrs. Szabo’s list had Miss Nowak here at ten. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. I sat down one stool away from her, which gave her room to decide about me. She had nails painted red and bitten, both. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ Miss Nowak looked at me for a while first, as if deciding what sort of question it was. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Miss Kahane was there at seven; Teitel was there at eight; Belkin was there at nine. Eight’s when I feel lucky. I don’t know why. It’s cost me a fortune. Then at ten I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door, with Belkin.” ¶ So here at ten and home at nine, which was what Belkin had said. At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it. ¶ Teitel had said he was here at nine, and that was worth the walk to the card room over Feingold’s garage. ¶ Sitting out a dance with her shoes in her lap: that was the last I saw of her.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “Miriam Hirsch,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Francis Doyle’s neighbor, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ Doyle was the alderman’s clerk. At half past eleven, Teitel, who’d come up for the Thursday card game, found the body in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ “When?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” Dr. Hirsch said. “The police surgeon puts it at nine or ten o’clock, by the warmth of him.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was Sokol’s, the same as every night,” she said. “The usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “Ask about Mrs. Pomerantz,” Dr. Hirsch said. “He had been at war with Mrs. Greco, her friend. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money and my hat, in that order.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. Doyle kept the papers in a box file, and I sat down with it under the lamp. ¶ The papers held a page on everybody with a grudge, kept like a doctor’s files, one grudge to a page and every page full. ¶ Miss Kahane: a complaint he’d made against her, in triplicate. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mrs. Pomerantz: a complaint against Mrs. Greco, with her name pencilled at the bottom. Miss Lowenthal: a note about her and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ Everybody in Doyle’s box had a reason. A reason isn’t a hand on the rat poison. ¶ I dusted off my knees. They’d done more work tonight than the rest of me.

Sokol was wiping flour off the gin bottles. ¶ I asked him who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven, I take the last tray out and unlock the door that says flour. One job stops, the other one starts. Seven o’clock, Mrs. Pomerantz. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Mrs. Pomerantz and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Ten, somebody in a camel coat, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. That’s everybody. I counted the glasses twice.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Sokol had Mrs. Pomerantz and Doyle at nine and somebody in a camel coat at ten. ¶ Slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. Dr. Hirsch had said nine or ten o’clock. The rat poison had come from the flats over Lipsky’s. I had an evening from Teitel, and a list from Sokol. I didn’t have Mrs. Pomerantz’s, Miss Kahane’s, Mrs. Krantz’s or Miss Lowenthal’s evenings yet. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

Miss Kahane’s flat was round the corner. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ Morning on Ludlow Street starts with the pickle man, who comes in from Brooklyn on the first car and rolls his barrels out onto the sidewalk with a sound like thunder in the next county. The Belvedere above him was waking to it floor by floor: a window going up, a baby starting, somebody’s alarm clock being argued with. There were five flights of stairs worn into a dip in the middle of every tread, with a gas jet turned low on each landing. ¶ Miss Kahane, in a fur collar, was folding leaflets on the bathtub board, a thousand of them, by lamplight. She had a cardboard suitcase of leaflets she carries everywhere, held shut with a belt. ¶ Wojcik’s list had Miss Kahane at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “I’ll answer you the way I answer everything: in writing, if you like, and in ink. At seven I went to the flats over Lipsky’s to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Teitel and Miss Lowenthal were there at seven; Miss Kahane, Teitel and Miss Lowenthal were there at eight; Teitel and Miss Lowenthal were there at nine. Eight, I do the arithmetic. It is never in my favor and never wrong. Come ten, I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play, with Russo.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Krantz said the card room over Feingold’s garage. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ It turned out Russo was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ Counting bills with a rubber thumb: that was the last I saw of her.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. I hadn’t slept since the night before the night before. The clock over the door had stopped pretending that mattered to it. I let it keep its own count. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ “It’s my late husband’s gold watch,” Feldman said. “It was under a glass dome on the parlor mantel, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “I sat in the Orpheum from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Eveready Hour, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want it badly enough to take it?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Whitfield,” he said. “He stood at my elbow at the Orpheum the whole time, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And he always said the watch was wasted on me.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Bidwell, a milliner, is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the watch would pawn for. And Hauck, an insurance agent, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Feldman said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where the watch is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

A few blocks west, and I was at the Orpheum. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Zeldin was in the lobby, counting the evening’s ticket stubs into bundles and putting a rubber band round each one. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Bidwell sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it. Hauck sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Zeldin. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Kowalski’s was round the corner. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Whitfield was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Abramowitz was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ Bidwell had said she was here at eight, with Abramowitz. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. The fee sat on the blotter where I’d dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “It’s my late husband’s gold watch,” Quill said. “I keep it under a glass dome on the parlor mantel, and it’s gone.” ¶ “I sat in the Kit Kat from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did the watch go missing?” ¶ He had it worked out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “It’s Vogel,” Quill said. “She stood at my elbow at the Kit Kat the whole time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the watch would pawn for.” ¶ He looked at the window, then back at me. “Feldman, a typist, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what the watch was worth. And Stannard, a bus conductor, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

The Kit Kat was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ I went up the outside stair to the Kit Kat, a speakeasy over a garage. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes. A glass globe hung from the ceiling with half its little mirrors gone, turning slowly over the dance floor. ¶ Ruggiero stood just inside the door with her back to the wall and her hands behind her. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Feldman sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. ¶ Ruggiero opens the door to everybody who comes in and shuts it behind everybody who goes, which means she sees the evening from about two feet away. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Rafferty’s lay a couple of blocks uptown and west. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Vogel was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Alfano was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ Feldman had said she was here at eight, with Vogel, and that was worth the walk. Mrs. Rafferty kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. A woman came in with a folder under her arm and the look of somebody used to being believed. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Abramowitz said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered her the chair and turned the lamp away from her. ¶ “I sat in Hanley’s from eight until ten,” she said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “And when did the cigarette case go missing?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” she said. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Atwater Kent Hour, which runs from eleven o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want it?” ¶ “It’s Winslow,” Abramowitz said. “He stood at my elbow at Hanley’s the whole time. And he says the cigarette case was promised to him by my late husband.” ¶ Then, almost as an afterthought: “Bidwell, an insurance agent, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill. And Zeldin, a milliner, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ She counted them off on her fingers without meaning to. “Renfro, a piano teacher, is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the cigarette case would pawn for.” ¶ Ten dollars came out of a pocket that had been saving it for something better. “Find out who. And get the cigarette case back.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

It was a fair few blocks to Hanley’s, uptown and east. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ Hanley’s, a saloon with sawdust on the floor, was the oldest bar on Houston Street and acted like it. The sawdust gets changed on Mondays whether it needs it or not, and it always needs it. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Prentiss was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Zeldin was on a stool with his hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Renfro had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Winslow sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Prentiss looks at everybody twice. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Zeldin had told me Hanley’s at eleven, and Prentiss’s list said otherwise. There was no going round it, so I didn’t. He saw the notebook in my hand and knew what it meant before I opened my mouth. ¶ “Here’s my trouble,” I said. “You told me Hanley’s at eleven. Prentiss had Renfro, Winslow and Lou at Hanley’s at eleven o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ Zeldin let out a long breath and sat down, as if his legs had decided it. “All right. I took it. It’s with Lou, a bookmaker who takes bets in the back booth. I owe Lou the bookmaker forty dollars.” ¶ So the cigarette case was with Lou, who was sitting ten feet away and hadn’t looked up once. That was what Abramowitz had paid for. ¶ Bidwell hadn’t told me his evening yet, and he was at the Delmonico rooms. ¶ The radio played on, low and cheerful, as if nothing had happened, which for the radio was true.

The card room was a good walk uptown and west. A milkman was leaving bottles on the steps, two by two, as quietly as a man can do anything with glass. ¶ The card room over the Bowery garage had no sign and no name on the door, only a light under it. A gambling room doesn’t advertise. The people who need it always find it. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Dandridge was shuffling a deck with one hand, not to play, just to keep the hand busy. Hands clasped in front, weight back on her heels, she stood as though poured there and left to set. ¶ A game is only as good as the people at it, so whoever runs one takes a good look at everybody who comes up the stairs. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

Crowninshield’s place was a few blocks downtown and east. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went to Crowninshield’s rooms behind the tailor’s on Allen Street. The passage from Allen Street smelled of pressed wool and machine oil, and it ended at a door the police had pulled shut on their way out. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Crowninshield lay on the floor on one side, where the fall had left the body, with the knees drawn up a little. ¶ Hochstetter let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

The Delmonico rooms were a couple of blocks downtown and east, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Tramonti sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bidwell was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. ¶ The revolver had come from here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

The Bijou lay a couple of blocks uptown and east. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Lathrop was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Hargrove was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. Colquitt was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Schilling sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Bidwell had said he was here at seven, and that Hargrove was with him at his place at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Lathrop. ¶ I stood at the back a moment, where the people who work a theater always stand.

A couple of blocks uptown, and I was at Sokol’s back room. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I went round to the back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where a nickel bet on a three-figure number bought you a reason to get up tomorrow. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Sweeney was at a table by the ovens, sorting slips of paper into piles by number. He had a good hat and cheap shoes, and was up on his toes the whole time, ready to be somewhere else. ¶ Whoever takes the slips sees everybody who puts down a nickel, and everybody does. ¶ The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

From there to Callahan’s place was a couple of blocks. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ Callahan’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street was one room at the top of the stairs. The police had been and gone, and the room had the look rooms get when a lot of people have stood in them and nobody sat down. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Callahan was in the chair with the head to one side, like somebody dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. ¶ Weisglass was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a few blocks to Moe’s, uptown and east. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Moe’s, a back-room bar behind a cigar store, was one room with no windows, a curtain for a door and a bar along one wall. After midnight it had the quiet of a place that expects to be quiet and is paid to be. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Hauck was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Ellery sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him. Stannard had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Crowninshield was standing at the bar with her coat over her arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Hauck looks at everybody twice. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Hauck’s list had Crowninshield here at seven, eight and ten, so I went over. I leaned on the bar next to her and ordered nothing, which got noticed. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ I asked Crowninshield to walk me through her night, every stop of it. She didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “I was at Moe’s from seven through eight. Ellery was there at seven; Stannard and Callahan were there at eight. Around nine I dropped a parcel off at Kowalski’s, with Ellery. At ten I went to Moe’s, as most nights, with Ellery. Walking over to Moe’s at ten I passed Pickering on Grand Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten and seven, with Ellery, which was what Hauck had. That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Grand Street was where Callahan lived. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.
