I went over to Bellucci and waited until he had a moment, which took a moment. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Stannard and somebody in the next seat I didn’t know. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Stannard here at ten, by his count. ¶ Ellery had said Pickering was with him at Kowalski’s at eight, and that was worth the walk to Pickering’s flat. ¶ My own hat had been reshaped by a few nights too. Not hot ones.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “My name is Thomas Kavanagh,” he said. “I was Alonzo Prentiss’s business partner. As of tonight I’m nobody’s.” ¶ The dead man had been a pawnbroker, and was found dead in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven. The one who found the body was Havemeyer, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When?” ¶ He said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “The coroner says laudanum in a drink, taken at nine or ten o’clock; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening, Moskowitz’s,” he said. “The usual. Never missed a night.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “There’s Bellucci,” Kavanagh said. “I don’t like gossip, but he owed Prentiss the rent on a shop, and it was being called in. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. The papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box people keep for the things they’d rather not file. ¶ There was a page on everybody with a grudge, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. They’d been kept square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Havemeyer: one line, where he was in 1921, and an address. Dettweiler: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted his sister a week before the wedding. Lathrop: the order that closed his business, with his signature on it. Sirkin: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. Bellucci: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. ¶ I put Prentiss’s pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the laudanum. ¶ The empty birdcage hung in its corner. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

Havemeyer had said he was here at eight and ten, and the landlady would know who’d been in. ¶ I went over to Mrs. Rafferty and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. I asked her to count the night for me, face by face. ¶ She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Lathrop, Dettweiler and Sirkin. Nobody else. Eight, Dettweiler, Sirkin and Havemeyer. Nobody else at all. Nine, Dettweiler and Sirkin. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Bellucci and Sirkin. Nobody else. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Mrs. Rafferty had Sirkin at both, Dettweiler at nine and Bellucci at ten. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Kavanagh had said nine or ten o’clock. The laudanum had come from Rafferty’s. I had an evening from Havemeyer, and a list from Mrs. Rafferty. I didn’t have Lathrop’s, Bellucci’s, Dettweiler’s or Sirkin’s evenings yet. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

Dettweiler didn’t get up when I came over, and didn’t ask me to sit, so I did both for him. I took the chair opposite Dettweiler and kept my hands where he could see them, on the tablecloth. “Mrs. Rafferty has you at Rafferty’s at seven and eight. I’d like the rest of your evening to go with it.” ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “At seven I went to Rafferty’s to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Lathrop and Sirkin were there at seven; Sirkin and Havemeyer were there at eight; Sirkin was there at nine. Then at ten I went to Moskowitz’s for a glass of tea, on my own.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, he said Moskowitz’s. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating.

I walked downtown and east to Lathrop’s flat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Lathrop’s flat on Pitt Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Lathrop, in a sailor’s pea coat, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, he kept his eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. ¶ Dettweiler had said Lathrop was with him at Rafferty’s at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. I hadn’t slept since the night before the night before. The clock over the door had stopped pretending that mattered to it. I let it keep its own count. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Russo said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “I had people in at eight,” he said, “for the burial society’s meeting. Kaminsky, Margolis and Amato. Nobody else came.” ¶ “The lock has been broken since Tuesday,” he said. “I showed the whole table the locksmith’s card.” ¶ “And when did the cigarette case go missing?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Atwater Kent Hour, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “I’ll give you a name,” he said. “Amato. He has always wanted the cigarette case, and asked me the price.” ¶ Then Russo went quieter, though there was nobody else in the room. “Margolis, the mechanic, says my IOU to him is overdue, and that the cigarette case would square it. And Kaminsky, the prizefighter, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk, in ones, smoothed flat. “Find out who took the cigarette case, and where to.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

It was a couple of blocks from there to Steinmetz’s, west, with my collar up. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Closing a chop house of the old kind takes an hour, and Steinmetz’s was in the middle of it: the chairs going up table by table, slowly, so as not to hurry anybody who might still order pie. The head waiter stood at his stand by the door, writing the last covers in his book in ink. The sawdust had been swept into the corners to think over what it had heard. There was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot, which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Margolis was wiping his hands on a rag that made them dirtier. Kaminsky was shadowboxing in a corner, very quietly, so as not to bother anybody. ¶ Margolis had been at Russo’s at eight, for the meeting. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.” ¶ Somebody went by with a plate of eggs, and my stomach reminded me it had been a long night.

The Lyric was a fair few blocks uptown. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Belkin was bowing to the empty seats with one hand on his heart. ¶ Kaminsky had said he was here at nine, with Belkin. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “From the back of the aisle I see the back of every head in the place, and the back of a head tells you more than a face: who leans, who doesn’t laugh, who keeps turning round to look at the doors.” ¶ The air smelled of dust and velvet and other people’s oranges.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. The fee sat on the blotter where I’d dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “It’s a pearl brooch,” Russo said. “I keep it in the dish on the dresser, and it’s gone.” ¶ “I had people in at eight for cards,” he said. “Kaminsky and Amato. Nobody else.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “And when did the brooch go?” ¶ “And I know when,” he said. “The dog next door went off at ten o’clock, the way it does when somebody’s on the stairs.” ¶ “Who’d want it?” ¶ “There’s Doyle,” he said. “I don’t like gossip, but he and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ He looked at the window, then back at me. “Amato, the cab driver, has always wanted the brooch, and asked me the price. And Kaminsky, the prizefighter, has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday.” ¶ Russo counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

The Lyric was a few blocks uptown and west. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There was the usher’s seating chart on a clipboard, every seat sold a pencil cross. ¶ Pinsky was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Kaminsky was eating a raw egg out of the shell, for the strength. ¶ Kaminsky had been at Russo’s at eight, for the card party. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “Nobody comes in late past me. They wait at the doors for the end of the scene like everybody else, and while they wait, I look at them.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

From there to Steinmetz’s was a fair few blocks. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Rain had driven the night’s last customers out of Steinmetz’s and the morning’s first ones hadn’t come. The chop house’s awning was sagging with a lake of water, which a waiter was poking up from underneath with a broom handle to watch it go over the edge in one piece, and then doing it again. There was the swinging door to the kitchen, with a porthole in it greased over so the dining room can’t see what goes into the chops. ¶ Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Miss Lowenthal was drinking tea from a cup with a saucer, always the saucer. ¶ Kaminsky had said he was here at nine. Pinsky’s list had Amato at the Lyric at nine, and that was worth the walk. From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I watch the door in the mirror over the bar. One sees who comes in without being seen to look, which is the whole of the profession.” ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. A woman came in with a folder under her arm and the look of somebody used to being believed. ¶ “It’s a set of silver spoons,” Miss Kahane said. “It was in the velvet box in the sideboard drawer, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered her the chair and turned the lamp away from her. ¶ “I had people in at eight,” she said, “to hear the fight on the radio. Amato, Miss Nowak and Doyle. Nobody else came.” ¶ “I went out after them,” she said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ She had it worked out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past eleven.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “There’s Kaminsky,” she said. “I don’t like gossip, but he says the spoons was promised to him, back in my courting days. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ There was more, and Miss Kahane didn’t much want to say it. “Miss Nowak, the switchboard operator, has always wanted the spoons, and asked me the price. And Amato, the cab driver, owes Margolis money, and he isn’t a patient man.” ¶ She looked at the ceiling for the next one, and found it there. “Doyle, the alderman’s clerk, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ She put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with her palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

From there to Rafferty’s was a couple of blocks. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was a row of umbrella hooks in the hall, each with a lodger’s name inked over it, and one with no name that nobody will explain. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was pouring tea nobody asked for. She had reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again. Miss Nowak was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. ¶ Miss Nowak had been at Miss Kahane’s at eight, for the fight party. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “Every lodger I have climbs those stairs his own way, and I know them all by it: two at a time, or stopping on the fourth for breath, or in his stocking feet thinking I’m asleep.” ¶ I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

Mabry was writing a tune on the back of an envelope. I asked him who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Eleven’s the hour for the last good tune. After that everybody’s playing for tips. Eleven o’clock, Miss Nowak and a drummer I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before eleven. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ Miss Nowak said home at eleven. The bandleader had her here at eleven o’clock. They couldn’t both be true, and Mabry had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ I wrote it down. Somebody whose job is watching a room doesn’t care who did what, only who came in, which makes them the best company in the city. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at eleven o’clock. Miss Nowak, Amato and Doyle were at the fight party and knew the way in; Kaminsky wasn’t. Miss Nowak had told me home at eleven, and Mabry’s list said otherwise. Amato, Kaminsky and Doyle hadn’t told me where they were at eleven, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out what Amato had to say for himself. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. ¶ I asked him to count the night for me, face by face. He went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight, the curtain goes up, and I go to the back of the house, where an usher belongs and an actor once didn’t. Mrs. Shapiro the wardrobe mistress was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, nobody else. Nine and ten, Amato and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Eleven, Kaminsky and Doyle. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ Amato said the Lyric at eleven. Pinsky had Kaminsky, Doyle and Mrs. Shapiro here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about him at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ Mouthing the third act from the back of the aisle: that was the last I saw of him.

Glick’s place was a fair few blocks uptown and east. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ It was cold on Ludlow Street and colder in the Belvedere, which has a stove in every kitchen and heat nowhere else. The hall smelled of brine from the shop and coal from the stoves, and on every landing a kitchen door stood open an inch for whatever warmth the stairs could spare, so the whole building listened to itself. There was a slot in the pickle store’s side door with LANDLORD painted over it, where the rent goes in on Saturdays and nothing ever comes back out. ¶ Glick was in the chair, sitting very still, the way nobody living ever sits for long. He had his collection book in his breast pocket, paid up to Friday, and a pencil behind each ear. ¶ Mrs. Ostrow let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the rat poison already in hand. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

It was a few blocks to the Lyric, west. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There were pigeons in the ventilator over the gallery, who coo in the quiet parts. ¶ Pinsky was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Mrs. Blau was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Mrs. Sobel was knitting a baby’s cap of no particular size. Mrs. Pomerantz was straightening the hat of the woman in front of her, unasked. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ Somebody had left a program on a seat. I didn’t read it. I had enough people to keep track of.

From there to the flats over Lipsky’s were a few blocks. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was eating a sandwich of black bread and onion out of a newspaper. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. Miss Lowenthal was winding a metronome. ¶ Mrs. Blau had said she was here at seven. Pinsky’s list had Miss Lowenthal at the Lyric at seven, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I know the tenants by their shoes. Faces, I don’t look at. A face can lie. A shoe has been where it’s been.” ¶ Somebody’s radio was going behind a door, low, so as not to wake anybody who was already awake.

The alley at Steinmetz’s was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ The alley behind Steinmetz’s was ash cans and crates and a puddle that never dries, lit by the kitchen door when it opened and by nothing when it didn’t. Somebody had made a bench out of an oyster crate and a plank, and the cobbles round it were thick with cigarette ends, where the kitchen does its thinking. There was the swinging door to the kitchen, with a porthole in it greased over so the dining room can’t see what goes into the chops. ¶ Tierney was picking a sliver of shell out of his thumb with a pin. He had a green bow tie and a voice like a priest at a christening. ¶ Tierney had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

From there to Russo’s place was a few blocks. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ The Excelsior stood on East Houston Street between a bank and a bakery, six floors of yellow brick with its name over the door and a lamp either side, the kind of building that puts on a necktie for the street. The lobby was tiled in black and white like a checkerboard, and somebody’s galoshes stood by the door in the middle of a game. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Russo was in the chair with the head to one side, like somebody dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. He had a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand. ¶ Dr. Hirsch was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a fair few blocks to the Peacock, uptown and west. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Mrs. Greco was telling her beads with flour still on her hands. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “I listen to the knock before I open the slot. A friend knocks twice and waits. A policeman knocks like he owns the door. A man with something to hide knocks once and starts talking.” ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Mrs. Szabo’s list had Mrs. Greco here at seven, eight and ten, so I went over. ¶ I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. She had a gold crucifix on a chain, and a burn on the inside of her wrist the shape of a ladle’s rim. I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ Mrs. Greco answered without looking at me, which is a way of answering. ¶ “My night. I was on my feet. Write that down first. I was at the Peacock from seven through eight. Teitel and Russo were there at seven; Kaminsky was there at eight. Nine o’clock I went to the flats over Lipsky’s to collect a debt, with Amato. Nine, my Rosa and the babies come into my head, and I get cross with whoever is closest. Then at ten I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door, with Amato. Walking over to the Peacock at ten I passed Kaminsky on East Houston Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten, with Amato, and here at seven, with Teitel and Russo, which was what Mrs. Szabo had. At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it. The part worth keeping came last. East Houston Street was where Russo lived. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline.

Margolis was stacking chips into a tray in fives. ¶ I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. Margolis went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Ten, the el stops for a minute and you can hear the chips. Then it starts again. Ten o’clock, Teitel and two men off the docks I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Teitel here at ten, by his count. ¶ Amato had said Kaminsky was with him at his place at seven, and that was worth the walk to Kaminsky’s flat. ¶ Wiping his hands on a rag that made them dirtier: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “My name is Leo Kaminsky,” he said. “I was Carmine Russo’s business partner. As of tonight I’m nobody’s.” ¶ Russo had been the card-room keeper, and was found dead in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found the body was Doyle, who’d come to settle a bet. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When?” ¶ He said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening, Sokol’s,” he said. “The usual. Never missed a night.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “There’s a letter from Mrs. Blau in the desk,” Kaminsky said. “It was on top, and I didn’t look any further. He knew what she got up to at Wexler’s, and let her know he knew.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. The papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box people keep for the things they’d rather not file. ¶ There was a page on everybody with a grudge, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. They’d been kept square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Dr. Hirsch: an IOU in her hand, and a note of what was still owing. Doyle: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Mrs. Greco: a copy of the family will, with her name underlined. Miss Lowenthal: an IOU from her friend, with her name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Blau: a note about her and Wexler’s, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ I put Russo’s pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the rat poison. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

Kaminsky had pointed me at Mrs. Blau. That was reason enough to ask. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. She had a voice that drops an octave when she wants it to, and a lace handkerchief she touches to her temples when the dead are being difficult. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “You want my evening. I felt you would. Sit. Take my hands. No? As you like. At seven I went to the flats over Lipsky’s to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Mrs. Greco and Dr. Hirsch were there at seven; Dr. Hirsch and Miss Lowenthal were there at eight; Dr. Hirsch was there at nine. Around ten I went over to Sokol’s for a drink, alone. Ten, I feel things. Tonight I felt a draft, mostly.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Blau said Sokol’s. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ Staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder: that was the last I saw of her.

The flats over Lipsky’s lay a few blocks uptown. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was the coal bin in the cellar, padlocked, with a chalk tally on the wall of whose scuttle got what, and two of the tallies rubbed out by a thumb. ¶ Wojcik was sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Doyle, in a fur collar, was handing out cigars with the alderman’s name on the band. Dr. Hirsch, in a grey fedora, was reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead. Miss Lowenthal, in a camel coat, was playing a nocturne very slowly with the soft pedal down. ¶ Mrs. Greco had said she was here at seven, and that Doyle was with her at Sokol’s at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

It was a couple of blocks to the stock room at the Peacock, west. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ The stock room behind the Peacock’s bar was crates of ginger ale stacked to the ceiling and, behind the ginger ale, crates of what the ginger ale was for. There was one chair, one bulb and a calendar from a funeral supply company with a different coffin for every month, and somebody had drawn a mustache on March. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Mabry was writing a tune on the back of an envelope. He had a pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been. ¶ Miss Lowenthal had said she was here at nine. That settled where I was going. ¶ Mabry had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Chandler Ainsworth,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Otto Wehrle’s cousin, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ Wehrle was a landlord, found dead in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven by Brauer, who heard his radio still going and knocked. The police put it down as his heart. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair. He took it, and held his hat on his knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ He had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “The woman across the hall heard him laughing with somebody all through the Eveready Hour, which runs from nine o’clock. The coroner says laudanum, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “I found a letter from Coffin in the desk,” he said. “He had been squeezing her for years. Start there.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Ainsworth said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

Brauer had found Wehrle, and I still didn’t know how she felt about any of it. I said who I was, and she took it about as well as people do. ¶ “Tell me about Wehrle,” I said to her. She let out a breath and told me what she thought. ¶ “Wehrle closed my business,” she said. “I still carry the key. I don’t know why. There’s nothing left for it to open.” ¶ That was Brauer’s reason, in her own words. Ainsworth hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. For nine, she had told me home at nine. ¶ The red lamp under the holy picture was still burning, for whoever needed it most.

The Orpheum lay a couple of blocks uptown and west. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight, had stopped the pictures for the night. Without one, a picture house is just three hundred red seats staring at a wall, which describes most of my evenings. The lobby carpet was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats. ¶ Havemeyer was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. He had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on his belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Coffin was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Sirkin was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. ¶ Havemeyer sees every face that comes in from the street, if only for the second it takes to look at a ticket. ¶ The air smelled of dust and velvet and other people’s oranges.

The Delmonico rooms were a fair few blocks downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ The Delmonico rooms again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Dettweiler sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. Brauer was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. Hanrahan was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Coffin had said she was here at eight, with Hanrahan. That settled where I was going. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. I didn’t have all of it. The form didn’t care. Forms never do. ¶ The rent envelope on my desk could stop worrying. For once I had something to put in it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Callahan. I took the stool next to him. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ He said he would tell me once, and I’d better be listening. ¶ “I was at work, at Feld’s studio at eight, with Corrigan. Then I locked up at nine and went to the Velvet Room to hear the fight on the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. At nine it was just me; Corrigan and Vitale were there at ten.” ¶ For nine, the hour that mattered, Callahan said the Velvet Room. It went in the notebook in his own words. ¶ It turned out Vitale was at the far end of the bar, nursing something. ¶ The table at Margolis’s place hadn’t been gone over yet. I wanted to see it before anybody tidied it. ¶ Even the cloudy mirror couldn’t make the night look any better, and it had been trying for years.

It was a few blocks from there to Feld’s studio, downtown and east, with my collar up. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ Feld’s photographic studio on Canal Street was shut for the night. The studio had a painted garden on the back wall and a velvet chair in front of it, for people to look their best in. A brass scale with a set of little weights stood at one end of the counter, perfectly balanced. ¶ Dandridge was tidying the shelves behind the counter, turning every label to face the front. ¶ Callahan had said he was here at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From behind his counter Dandridge can see the door and everybody who uses it. ¶ I stood out of the way, which in a place like that is a job in itself.

It was a couple of blocks to Feld’s studio, downtown. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Back at Feld’s studio, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Dandridge was behind the counter, writing in a ledger by the light of a green-shaded lamp. ¶ I looked at the brass scale again. Everything weighs something, if you have the little weights.

The Shamrock lay a good walk downtown and east. A man was selling chestnuts on the corner, and the fog stood round his brazier like customers who weren’t buying. ¶ The Shamrock, a bar on the corner, had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that Avenue B could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to. Behind the bar a moose head with one glass eye looked out over the bottles, having seen it all and liked none of it. ¶ Dettweiler was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Bellucci was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. Steinbach had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Quill sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of her. ¶ Callahan had been here earlier in the evening. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. From behind a bar you can see the whole room and the door, and that side of the bar belonged to Dettweiler. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

Bellucci had said Quill was with him here at ten, and I still didn’t know what she thought about any of it. I took the stool beside her and let her finish her drink before I spoiled it. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, she kept her eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. ¶ I mentioned Callahan to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. She let out a breath and told me what she thought. ¶ “Callahan jilted my sister a week before the wedding,” she said. “She cried for a month, and I heard every minute of it through the wall.” ¶ That was Quill’s reason, in her own words. Hurwitz hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

I sat down near Sirkin, in a corner nobody else was using. ¶ I asked Sirkin to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ She told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “I was at the Shamrock from seven through eight, with Quill and Callahan. Come nine, I went home to change, and stayed the rest of the evening. Bellucci was there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ So home at nine, which was what Bellucci had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said home at the Delmonico rooms. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ I still hadn’t looked properly at the table at Callahan’s place. ¶ The humming stopped short of the end again. I’d have paid a nickel to hear how it came out.

I set off uptown and west for the Palace. It was a good walk. I could still smell the chestnut man’s brazier, or thought I could. It was the warmest thing that had happened to me all night. ¶ The Palace again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Sirkin was sitting where she could see the door, with her hat on and her coat buttoned. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

It was a fair few blocks to Callahan’s place, uptown. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ Callahan’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street was as high up as the building went. The police had been and gone, and left the place with its lamp lit and its door shut, like a shop on a holiday. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Callahan was in the chair with the head to one side, like somebody dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. ¶ Hurwitz was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ If it happened at ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the laudanum already in hand. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

Kowalski’s was a fair few blocks uptown and east, and I took it at a good clip. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Petrosino was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Bernstein had pointed me at Petrosino. That settled where I was going. Mrs. Kowalski kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Mrs. Kowalski’s list had Petrosino here at seven, and I still didn’t know how she felt about any of it. She sat me down at the kitchen table, under a light that was hard on both of us. ¶ I asked her about Ruggiero. She looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Ruggiero jilted my sister a week before the wedding,” she said. “She cried for a month, and I heard every minute of it through the wall.” ¶ That was Petrosino’s reason, in her own words. Bernstein hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. For nine and ten, she had told me the Kit Kat at nine and home at ten. ¶ The sign in the hall still said the hot water was by arrangement. Everything in this city is.

Kowalski’s was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Kowalski’s looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. Petrosino was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Ruggiero’s place was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ I went back to Ruggiero’s place, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Bernstein let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Ruggiero had died here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ The calendar went on saying last month. In that room, it might as well.

Ruggiero’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ Back at Ruggiero’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Bernstein had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. It was reason enough to look. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Brauer was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from him yet. That was one thing. How Brauer felt about the whole business was another, and I wanted to hear it. I sat down where he could see me, and didn’t hurry. ¶ I said Kessler’s name and watched what Brauer’s face did with it. He answered as if he’d been asked before, by somebody, about something. ¶ “I owed Kessler four hundred dollars,” he said. “Four hundred. I used to say it in my sleep.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Lefkowitz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

Brauer had said Wehrle was with him at the Delmonico rooms at nine. I wanted to hear the other side of it. ¶ I sat down across from her with a cup of coffee for company. She smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept her gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. I asked Wehrle where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “I was home at the Delmonico rooms from seven through nine. Salerno was there at seven; Schilling was there at eight; Brauer was there at nine. Ten o’clock I went to Moskowitz’s for the blue-plate supper, with Brauer.” ¶ So home at nine and here at ten, which was what Brauer had said. At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it. ¶ I could have used gloves like that. Mine have all ten fingertips, and they still let the cold in.

I headed downtown and west for the Delmonico rooms, a few blocks away. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Abramowitz was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ Salerno had said she was here at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Abramowitz had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I passed the holy picture on the stairs and kept my eyes front. I don’t like being looked at that kindly.

It was a good walk to Moskowitz’s, uptown and west. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I went back to Moskowitz’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Bernstein stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Brauer was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Wehrle sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Schilling was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. ¶ Salerno had said she was here at eight. Wehrle had said Schilling was with her at her place at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and east to the Delmonico rooms, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ The Delmonico rooms again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Abramowitz sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. ¶ The revolver had come from here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Corrigan had pointed me at Carbone. Where is only half of it. The other half is why. I sat down where she could see me, and didn’t hurry. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ I said Lanza’s name and watched what her face did with it. She let out a breath and told me what she thought. ¶ “Lanza testified against my brother,” she said. “Stood up in court in a new suit and did it. I remember the suit.” ¶ That was Carbone’s reason, in her own words. Corrigan hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I didn’t waste Havemeyer’s time. He looked like somebody who kept count of it. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. He didn’t ask why I wanted it. He just let me know it cost something. ¶ “At seven I went to Rafferty’s for the company, and stayed through nine. Hochstetter and Carbone were there at seven; Hochstetter, Carbone and Dettweiler were there at eight; Hochstetter and Carbone were there at nine. At ten I went round to Dettweiler’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Havemeyer said Rafferty’s at nine and Dettweiler’s flat at ten. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

Hochstetter had been watching me ask the others, and had had time to think about it, which isn’t always an advantage. ¶ I sat down near her, in a corner nobody else was using. ¶ I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. She had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Carbone and Havemeyer were there at seven; Carbone, Dettweiler and Havemeyer were there at eight; Carbone and Havemeyer were there at nine. Then at ten I went to the Palace to sit through the double bill, with Kavanagh.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Hochstetter said home at nine and the Palace at ten. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ It turned out Kavanagh was three rows back with her hat over her eyes. ¶ I read the old cough syrup sign again. Relief guaranteed. I’d have settled for less.

Dettweiler’s flat was a good walk east. Cannon Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Back at Dettweiler’s flat, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Dettweiler, in a fur collar, answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. ¶ Hochstetter had said Dettweiler was with her at her place at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

It was a few blocks from there to Dettweiler’s flat, east, with my collar up. The rain was letting up as the sky went gray, as if it had only come out to keep the night company. ¶ Back at Dettweiler’s flat, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Dettweiler, in a fur collar, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ Somebody’s radio was going behind a door, low, so as not to wake anybody who was already awake.

It was a few blocks to the flats over Lipsky’s, uptown and east. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ It was a clear night over Orchard Street, the kind that shows you every washing line strung between the buildings, and the tenement over Lipsky’s had more than its share. A whole family’s shirts hung out over the street on a pulley, white as a surrender, waiting for a sun that wasn’t due till six. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Mrs. Sobel was drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth. ¶ Belkin had pointed me at Mrs. Sobel. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Glick’s place was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ By that hour the Belvedere had gone dark from the pickle store to the roof, every flat but one, where a kitchen light was on and a kettle was beginning to think about it. The stairs creaked under nobody at all, the way old stairs do at night, settling the day’s accounts. There were pickle barrels along the shop front, chained shut for the night, with a sign on the lid, DO NOT TOUCH, that has never once worked. ¶ Glick was in the chair by the table, head down on folded arms, like somebody asleep over the accounts. He had his collection book in his breast pocket, paid up to Friday, and a pencil behind each ear. ¶ Belkin, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ If it happened at ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the rat poison already in hand. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. I asked him for everybody he’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because he liked them. ¶ He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight, I sit. Pipe. Steps. Street. Eight o’clock, Mrs. Blau, Mrs. Sobel and Amato. Nobody else. Nine, Mrs. Blau, Mrs. Sobel, Mrs. Ostrow and Amato. Nobody else at all. Ten, Mrs. Sobel and Amato. Nobody else. A rat. A rat doesn’t count. The rat poison on the cellar shelf was there at eight. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Wojcik had Mrs. Sobel here at eight, same as she said. I wrote down what the list had at ten, the hour that mattered: Mrs. Sobel and Amato. ¶ Mrs. Ostrow could tell me her own evening, and she was at the Peacock. ¶ Knocking his pipe out on his boot heel and looking at nothing: that was the last I saw of him.

It was a couple of blocks from there to the flats over Lipsky’s, east, with my collar up. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I went back to the flats over Lipsky’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Wojcik was sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago. Mrs. Sobel was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Amato answered the door in his stocking feet, with the lamp behind him. ¶ Sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe: that was the last I saw of him.

Getting to Sokol’s meant a couple of blocks uptown. Rivington Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Sokol’s sold bread at the front and gin at the back. After midnight you went through the dark bakery, past ovens still warm and racks of tomorrow’s rolls rising under cloths, to a door with FLOUR painted on it. Behind the door were six stools, four tables and a radio playing dance music low, so it wouldn’t get into the bread. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. ¶ Sokol was looking in on the ovens through the door marked FLOUR. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Dr. Hirsch was drinking a brandy at the bar with a medical journal propped on the bottles. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. ¶ Teitel had found Doyle. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.” ¶ Somebody laughed at the far end of the bar, and it wasn’t at me, for once.

It was a couple of blocks from there to Doyle’s place, downtown and east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Behind its own front door the Excelsior was asleep: a good door, with a brass knob and a wooden wedge holding it open an inch for some tenant who keeps losing his key. The lobby mirror gave me back a man who needed a shave and a better coat. Nobody watches this door; that’s what the tenants pay for. There was a dumbwaiter in the back hall for coal and parcels, with a bell on every floor that nobody answers. ¶ Doyle was in the chair by the table, where the police had left the body, chin down like somebody resting tired eyes for a minute. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Mrs. Krantz, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ If it happened at nine, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the chloral already in hand. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Amato. There were ashtrays that are never emptied, only added to, so that there are eleven of them now. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter. At eight I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play, and I was there all evening. Nobody was with me, any of it. Nine’s dead. Nine’s always dead. You could roll a bowling ball down Delancey at nine.” ¶ For nine, the hour that mattered, Amato said the card room over Feingold’s garage. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ Teitel’s evening was still a blank in my notebook, and he was at Sokol’s. ¶ Watching the game over a man’s shoulder with his cap pushed back: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My head ached from the night before. I’d sent two aspirin after it, and they hadn’t found it yet. The fog outside made the street lamp a smudge, and my eyes were grateful. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor talked the whole walk to the chair: her sister, her landlord, and eventually the reason she’d come. ¶ “I’m Tillie Moskin,” she said, sitting down on the edge of the chair. “I was Lazar Belkin’s clerk. The police have been and gone, and that’s all they did.” ¶ The dead man had been the leading man, and was found dead in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found the body was Mrs. Blau, who’d come to settle a bet. The police wrote it down as a robbery gone wrong. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ Miss Moskin had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “Shot at nine o’clock: the woman below took it for a backfire, just after the nine o’clock el went by.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Start with Miss Kahane,” Miss Moskin said. “She and Belkin had been at each other’s throats for years.” ¶ She counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Blau. ¶ I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “The spirits keep strange hours, and so do I. But I’ll tell you mine. I was at Sokol’s at seven, with Mrs. Krantz and Miss Kahane. Eight o’clock I went up to Rafferty’s to see about some money owed, with Miss Kahane. Eight, I sit very still and wait for somebody to speak. Usually it’s the people downstairs. Then at nine I stopped in at Sokol’s to get warm. Come ten, I went round to the little room at Wexler’s to see about a pledge. Nobody was with me at nine or ten.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Blau said the little room at Wexler’s. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ The floor at Belkin’s place hadn’t been gone over yet. I wanted to see it before anybody tidied it. ¶ People always remember their own evenings well. It’s other people’s they go vague on.

Rafferty’s was a couple of blocks east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was a row of umbrella hooks in the hall, each with a lodger’s name inked over it, and one with no name that nobody will explain. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open. She had reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. ¶ Mrs. Blau had said she was here at eight. Mrs. Krantz had said Miss Nowak was with her at Sokol’s at eight. That settled where I was going. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “I sit on the first landing with the mending till the last one’s in, and nobody gets up my stairs without stepping over the basket.” ¶ The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

The little room at Wexler’s was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at the little room at Wexler’s. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Mrs. Blau had a chair in the corner and a cup of coffee, and the look of somebody who would say she was only passing. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I walked west to Sokol’s. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ Sokol’s again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Sokol was wiping flour off the gin bottles. Mrs. Krantz was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Miss Kahane was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at eight. Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Miss Kahane at Rafferty’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Rubbing his eyes with the heels of both hands, like a man trying to put them back: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My jaw had gone from purple to a color nobody sells paint in. Even the low lamp showed that much. The mirror could wait for morning. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor talked the whole walk to the chair: her sister, her landlord, and eventually the reason she’d come. ¶ “Minna Blau,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Lazar Belkin’s old sweetheart, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ The dead man was the leading man, found dead in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven by Miss Nowak, who’d come up for the Thursday card game. The police put it down as his heart. ¶ “When was this?” ¶ Mrs. Blau said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “The police surgeon puts it at nine or ten o’clock, by the warmth of him.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was Steinmetz’s, the same as every night,” she said. “The usual.” ¶ “Who’d have wanted that?” ¶ “Ask about Miss Kahane,” Mrs. Blau said. “She and Belkin had been at each other’s throats for years. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

Miss Nowak had found Belkin, and I still didn’t know what she thought about any of it. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. ¶ I asked her whether there was anything I ought to know where he was concerned. “I’m sorry, that line’s busy.” ¶ “Belkin had been at war with my friend.” ¶ That was Miss Nowak’s reason, in her own words. Mrs. Blau hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. For nine and ten, she had told me the band room at the Peacock at nine and home at ten. ¶ Writing a letter home to Scranton: that was the last I saw of her.

Rafferty’s was a couple of blocks uptown, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ Rafferty’s looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was counting the umbrellas on their hooks. Miss Nowak was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at seven and ten. That was reason enough. ¶ Saying a decade of the rosary under her breath, with one eye open: that was the last I saw of her.

It was a couple of blocks to Rafferty’s, uptown and east. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ Rafferty’s again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink. Miss Nowak was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. ¶ There was Parnell, a ginger cat, asleep on a different stair every time anybody comes in, as if he were keeping count for her.

Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Mrs. Krantz at Rafferty’s at eight and nine. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. She had a pince-nez on a black ribbon, which she puts on to read a rent book and takes off to read a face. ¶ I said Belkin’s name and watched what her face did with it. “I collect rents. I don’t collect gossip; it doesn’t pay on the first.” ¶ “Mr. Belkin borrowed a hundred dollars from me in a voice that made it sound like a favor to me.” ¶ That was Mrs. Krantz’s reason, in her own words. Mrs. Blau hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ Counting bills with a rubber thumb: that was the last I saw of her.

Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ Steinmetz’s had its name in gold on the window, CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS, lit from below by the lamps on the oyster bar, and behind it a long room going quietly about the last orders of the night. The waiters wore white aprons to the ankle, which made them look as if they were standing in buckets, and the tables near the door were already stripped to the wood. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Dr. Hirsch was smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. ¶ Kaminsky had been here earlier in the evening. That settled where I was going. From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I headed east for Dr. Hirsch’s surgery, a couple of blocks away. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The dentist’s rooms over the bank were dark except the frosted door, which glowed a little from the streetlamp behind it. The waiting room had six chairs, a rubber plant and a table of magazines, and the rubber plant looked the most patient. There was a cylinder of laughing gas on a trolley, with a rubber mask that has seen a great many faces at their worst. ¶ Miss Gutman was reading a movie magazine with her lips pressed shut. She had a bob she cut herself with the surgery scissors, a little shorter on the left. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had said she was here at seven and eight. That was reason enough. ¶ From her post Miss Gutman could see the waiting room and the stairs up from the street. “I can tell a patient from a visitor on the stairs. A patient comes up slow and holds his jaw. A visitor comes up quick and holds his hat.” ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Miss Gutman’s list had Russo at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery at eight, and I still didn’t know how he felt about any of it. He let me in as far as the kitchen, which in that house was as far as anybody got. ¶ I mentioned Kaminsky to Russo and let the quiet do some of the asking. “That’s a side bet. I don’t take side bets.” ¶ “The kid owes me forty from a hand he shouldn’t have played. I don’t press a fighter. A fighter presses back.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Amato hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ Sitting with his back to the wall: that was the last I saw of him.

Russo’s flat was a fair few blocks downtown and east. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ Russo’s flat again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Russo was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

It was a few blocks to Kaminsky’s place, east. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Morning on Ludlow Street starts with the pickle man, who comes in from Brooklyn on the first car and rolls his barrels out onto the sidewalk with a sound like thunder in the next county. The Belvedere above him was waking to it floor by floor: a window going up, a baby starting, somebody’s alarm clock being argued with. There were five flights of stairs worn into a dip in the middle of every tread, with a gas jet turned low on each landing. ¶ Kaminsky sat in the chair with both hands in the lap. If you didn’t know, you’d have said asleep, and lowered your voice. He had his hands still taped, and a fight program in his pocket with his name spelled wrong. ¶ Amato, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ There was a speaking tube by the street door with a brass whistle for every floor, which hasn’t carried a word since 1911, and which every visitor blows into anyway.

Getting to the flats over Lipsky’s meant a few blocks uptown and east. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were five floors of brick on Orchard Street, with the cloth shop shut up at the bottom behind iron shutters. After midnight the pushcarts stood along the curb under their tarpaulins, waiting for morning. Down by the cellar steps under the stoop a pipe glowed and went dark: the janitor was still on his steps, or had left the pipe to do it for him. There was the coal bin in the cellar, padlocked, with a chalk tally on the wall of whose scuttle got what, and two of the tallies rubbed out by a thumb. ¶ Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Teitel, with a cane, was haggling with a customer who had already paid. Mrs. Blau, in a green hat, was touching a lace handkerchief to her temples, as if somebody were calling. Mrs. Krantz, with a bandaged hand, was looking at a banister as if it owed her money. ¶ Teitel had found Doyle. That was reason enough. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “The stoop has five steps, and the fourth one rings when you stand on it. I don’t fix it.” ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

Teitel had said Mrs. Krantz was with him at his place at seven, and I still didn’t know what she thought about any of it. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. She was a stout woman in gray, buttoned to the throat, carrying a leather satchel with a brass lock on it. ¶ I asked her straight out about Doyle, and waited. “I collect rents. I don’t collect gossip; it doesn’t pay on the first.” ¶ “Francis Doyle courted me for a year in nineteen-four and then married the alderman’s niece. He’s been an alderman’s clerk ever since. I call that justice.” ¶ That was Mrs. Krantz’s reason, in her own words. Belkin hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ Reading the names on the mailboxes with her pince-nez on: that was the last I saw of her.

Russo was counting a stack of bills by the edge. “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” ¶ He counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Ten, everybody I know starts needing a loan. I give it. I remember it. Ten o’clock, Teitel and two men off the docks I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ The hours that mattered were nine and ten. Russo had Teitel and two men off the docks nobody could put a name to at ten and nobody at nine. ¶ Dealing himself a hand of solitaire: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Belkin had said nine or ten o’clock. I had evenings from Teitel and Mrs. Blau, and a list from Russo. I didn’t have Mrs. Sobel’s or Mrs. Krantz’s evenings yet. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

The flats over Lipsky’s were only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. I wondered if the cab driver was still asleep at the curb.
