Somebody in this city ought to be. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Wojcik was sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe. Teitel, with a cane, was arranging neckties on the kitchen table by color, then by price, then by color again. Mrs. Blau, in a green hat, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. Mrs. Krantz, with a bandaged hand, was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. ¶ Mrs. Blau had said she was here at ten, with Mrs. Krantz. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

It was no distance to Sokol’s: round the corner, and there it was. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The bakery half of Sokol’s had woken up and the bar half had gone to bed. The ovens had the shop warm enough to steam the window, and the first trays of rolls were coming out. The door marked FLOUR was shut, with a sack of real flour leaning on it as an alibi. There was a radio on the shelf behind the bar, turned low so the music won’t get into the bread. ¶ Sokol was rubbing his eyes with the heels of both hands, like a man trying to put them back. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Mrs. Sobel, in a sailor’s pea coat, was drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth. ¶ Mrs. Blau had said she was here at seven, eight and nine. Teitel had said Mrs. Sobel was with him at his place at seven. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “A man drinks the same thing on the same stool every night of his life. When the stool is empty, I notice. When a stranger sits on it, I notice twice.” ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ “Somebody has taken my Pomeranian,” Vitale said. “Duchess. Gone from her cushion by the radiator, just like that.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “I had people in at eight for the burial society’s meeting,” he said. “Pickering, Mulcahy and Broadnax. Nobody else.” ¶ “The parlor window onto the fire escape won’t latch,” he said. “I showed everybody at the table. I laughed about it.” He wasn’t laughing now. ¶ “When did you last see her?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past ten.” ¶ “Anybody you can think of who’d want Duchess?” ¶ “Start with Pickering,” he said. “He owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ Then, almost as an afterthought: “Mulcahy, a bus conductor, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Duchess was worth. And Broadnax, a shoe clerk, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Vitale said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where Duchess is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

The Shamrock was a good walk downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The stars were out over the rooftops, which in this city means somebody forgot to switch something on. ¶ The Shamrock, a bar on the corner, had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that Avenue B could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Ellery was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Mulcahy was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. Pickering sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him. ¶ From behind a bar you can see the whole room and the door, and that side of the bar belonged to Ellery. ¶ The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at the Orpheum. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. The lobby carpet was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats. ¶ Crowninshield was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Broadnax was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Sweeney sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Pickering had said he was here at nine, with Sweeney. It was reason enough to look. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Crowninshield. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. The mirror over the washbasin showed more of the night before than I wanted explained. I turned the lamp away from it. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor hung up his own coat and sat like a man who’d waited in better rooms and billed for it. ¶ “Caruso’s gone,” Sweeney said. “My roller canary. He sleeps in his cage by the window, and he isn’t there.” ¶ “I sat in the Shamrock from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did Caruso go missing?” ¶ “And I know when,” he said. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the A&P Gypsies, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want him?” ¶ “You might ask about Ruggiero,” he said. “She is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a roller canary with papers fetches. That’s from the woman downstairs, and she hears most things.” ¶ Then Sweeney went quieter, though there was nobody else in the room. “Quill, a bookmaker, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind. And Feeney, a typist, has wanted Caruso since the day I brought him home.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money. It was the first good news of the night, and I was making the most of it.

The Shamrock was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ The Shamrock, a bar on the corner, had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that Avenue B could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Lathrop was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Quill was in a booth by the wall, alone with a glass of beer and a newspaper. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it. ¶ Somewhere on the radio a band was having a better night than I was.

I walked uptown and west to Rafferty’s. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step. On the landing a rubber plant had grown up to the ceiling and was thinking about going further. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Ruggiero was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Zeldin was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. ¶ Quill had said he was here at eight, and that Ruggiero was with him at the Shamrock at nine. That settled where I was going. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Rafferty had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

A couple of blocks uptown and east, and I was at the Havemeyer flat. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went up to the Havemeyer flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue. A narrow stair, a landing with one door on it, and on the door a nameplate that somebody had polished thin. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Havemeyer had left everything just as it was, so that Duchess would know the way home. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If she went at eleven, she went after the supper, and everybody at the supper had known the way in. ¶ It was quiet there in the way that makes you lower your voice when there’s nobody to hear it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Salerno. ¶ I leaned on the bar next to him and ordered nothing, which got noticed. Young and tidy and a little tired, he still had the mark of the headset band pressed into his hair. I asked him to walk me through his night, every stop of it. ¶ Salerno put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “I was at Havemeyer’s at eight, for the supper, with Rosenbaum and Callahan. Nine o’clock I left the supper to get some air and went to the Kit Kat to see who was about, with Rosenbaum. Then at ten I went to the Palace to sit through the double bill. Come eleven, I went down to the Kit Kat to hear the trumpet. At ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ So the Havemeyer flat at eight, with Rosenbaum and Callahan, which was what Havemeyer had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For eleven, the hour that mattered, he said the Kit Kat. It went in the notebook in his own words. ¶ Pickering had been there all night, and would know who came and went. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

It was no distance to the Palace: round the corner, and there it was. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went in at the back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street. It was a big shabby picture house with the gilt coming off the plaster, and the back row sat under the balcony, where the light from the screen never quite reached. A bare bulb hung on a cord, swinging a little whenever the door shut. ¶ Shapiro stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Shapiro. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Mrs. Rafferty saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Mulcahy. Nobody else. Nine, Callahan and Mulcahy. Nobody else at all. Ten, Mulcahy. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, nobody but me.” ¶ Callahan said home at eleven. Mrs. Rafferty had nobody here at eleven o’clock. One of them was wrong. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.
I sat down with the form and a pencil. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ The office lamp was the best listener I’d had all night, and I include me.

I went over Ruggiero’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ Brennan turned his back while I worked, and I was grateful. I don’t like an audience for this part. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to Kowalski’s. Somebody had made the dead man cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from Kowalski’s, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Ruggiero had been at Kowalski’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Ruggiero’s place yet, and papers go on talking after the one who kept them has stopped. ¶ I put everything back where it had been, as near as I could.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Fairbanks. I asked him for a minute, and he gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” Fairbanks counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Prentiss, Carbone and Ruggiero. Nobody else. Eight, Corrigan and Carbone. Nobody else at all. Nine, Carbone and Ruggiero. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Sirkin and Carbone. Nobody else.” ¶ Carbone hadn’t been at Kowalski’s while it was there to take. That put Sirkin and Carbone here at ten, by his count. Brennan had said nine or ten. Ruggiero was at Moskowitz’s at nine, alive. ¶ Corrigan was right here, and I didn’t have his evening yet. ¶ I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things.

I went over to Mrs. Kowalski and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “All of them, hour by hour, and who you didn’t know.” She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Corrigan and Sirkin. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Prentiss and Sirkin. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody but me. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Prentiss, Corrigan and Sirkin had been here earlier, when the laudanum was there for the taking. Mrs. Kowalski had him here at seven, same as he said. At ten, when it counted, the list had nobody. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

I waited for a gap in Hargrove’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. ¶ Hargrove went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Corrigan and two men off the docks I didn’t know. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Corrigan here at ten, by his count. ¶ Whatever had been poured there had set by then. I walked round it.

It was a few blocks from there to Donnelly’s place, east, with my collar up. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Donnelly’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street was as high up as the building went. The police had been and gone, and left the place with its lamp lit and its door shut, like a shop on a holiday. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Donnelly lay by the door, back to the room, as if on the way somewhere and stopped. ¶ My client, Whitfield, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in his hand. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I walked west to the Velvet Room. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ The Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop, had a door you had to knock on, which on Elizabeth Street is a formality. Everybody knows the knock, and the hats in the window upstairs have heard it so often they could do it themselves. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Zeldin was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Dandridge was at the bar with a drink she wasn’t drinking. Rosenbaum was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Weisglass was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Zeldin looks at everybody twice. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Zeldin’s list had Dandridge here at seven, eight and ten. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. I took the stool next to her. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” Dandridge thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I was at the Velvet Room from seven through eight. Donnelly was there at seven; Rosenbaum and Donnelly were there at eight. Come nine, I went round to the Delmonico rooms to borrow a collar stud, with Weisglass. Around ten I went to the Velvet Room, as most nights, with Weisglass. Walking over to the Velvet Room at ten I passed Lanza on Ludlow Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten, with Weisglass, and here at seven, with Donnelly, which was what Zeldin had. One evening that held, at an hour that mattered, where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Ludlow Street was where Donnelly lived. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

Lanza let me in as far as the kitchen, which in that house was as far as anybody got. ¶ “Mr. Lanza, I’m asking everybody the same thing. Where were you tonight?” He asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “I was home at seven. Come eight, I dropped a parcel off at the Delmonico rooms, with Weisglass. Around nine I went home to iron a shirt for the morning, and stayed the rest of the evening. At seven, nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ He said home at ten. Dandridge passed him on Ludlow Street at ten. One of them was wrong. The rest held where I could check it: Weisglass had him at the Delmonico rooms at eight, same as he said. ¶ Rosenbaum had said she was here at nine, and that was worth the walk to the Eagle club office. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I found somewhere to sit and took out the form. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ The office telephone never had rung tonight. It hadn’t needed to. The trouble had taken the stairs.

I went over Weisglass’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ Donnelly didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to the Delmonico rooms. Somebody had made the dead man cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from the Delmonico rooms, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Weisglass had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Bledsoe. ¶ I waited for a gap in his night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked him to take me through the night, hour by hour, everybody in the place. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Alfano, Hochstetter and Weisglass. Nobody else. Eight, Alfano and Bernstein. Nobody else at all. Nine, Alfano and Weisglass. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, somebody in a green hat, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. Nobody else.” ¶ At nine and ten, when it counted, Bledsoe had Alfano and Weisglass at nine and somebody in a green hat at ten. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

Mrs. Quill saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. I asked her who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. ¶ She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Bernstein and Prentiss. Nobody else. Eight, Hochstetter, Petrosino and Prentiss. Nobody else at all. Nine, Hochstetter and Prentiss. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Alfano and Prentiss. Nobody else. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Quill had Alfano and Prentiss. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

I went over to Moretti and waited until he had a moment, which took a moment. ¶ I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. He went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Bernstein and a man from uptown I didn’t know. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ I wrote down what Moretti had at ten, the hour that mattered: Bernstein and a man from uptown nobody could put a name to. ¶ I read the old cough syrup sign again. Relief guaranteed. I’d have settled for less.

I found a chair at Petrosino’s flat and sat down with the form. I put down what I had, and what I had would have to stand up by itself. ¶ The new money would go in the desk drawer with the old. The drawer had never had company before.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Mrs. Krantz sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over her own parlor like a stranger’s. ¶ The cushion by the radiator was empty. The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Mrs. Krantz at Steinmetz’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Steinmetz’s the place to start counting. ¶ The one to ask was the head waiter at Steinmetz’s, who’d been there all night. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

Amato was at the same table, working through a slice of pie as if it owed him money. ¶ There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. Amato was a stocky man in a leather jacket and a chauffeur’s cap pushed back, moving a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other to show he’s thinking. ¶ “Demos has you here at nine. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Mrs. Pomerantz and Miss Moskin. Eight, I eat. Most men eat sitting at a table. I’m not most men. Nine o’clock I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Doyle, Mrs. Pomerantz and Lieb. Then at ten I went to the Lyric, because a friend was in the show, alone.” ¶ So here at nine, with Doyle, Mrs. Pomerantz and Lieb, which was what Demos had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said the Lyric. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ The usher at the Lyric would know who’d been in. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

I took an aisle seat at the Lyric and did my paperwork by the light from the doors. Every question on it had an answer, and every answer had a name and an hour behind it. ¶ My head was still keeping time with the clock over the office safe, a little behind and a lot louder.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Mrs. Pomerantz told me twice where everything usually was. I let her. It was her flat, and it was the only thing she could do. ¶ The basket by the stove was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Mrs. Pomerantz at Steinmetz’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Steinmetz’s the place to start counting. ¶ The head waiter at Steinmetz’s sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ There was a speaking tube by the street door with a brass whistle for every floor, which hasn’t carried a word since 1911, and which every visitor blows into anyway.

Demos’s list had Glick here at nine. I wanted to hear the other side of it. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. He had a little leather book of weekly payments in his breast pocket, and the habit of patting it, the way other men pat for a wallet. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ He counted back through the evening under his breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “Certainly. A man in my line is always glad to account for himself. It’s other people’s accounts that keep me up. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Miss Moskin. Eight, I think about mortality. Professionally. Nine o’clock I went to Steinmetz’s for supper, and stayed the rest of the evening. Miss Lowenthal was there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Glick said Steinmetz’s at ten. Demos had Tierney here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about him at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ Polishing his derby with his sleeve: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Glick and Miss Lowenthal were at Steinmetz’s while Mrs. Pomerantz told the room; Mrs. Ostrow wasn’t. Glick had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Ostrow and Miss Lowenthal hadn’t told me where they were at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Tierney, the oyster opener at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Glick now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

I sat down in the back row with the form on my knee. I put down what I had, and what I had would have to stand up by itself. ¶ The mirror over my washbasin could wait for morning. One of us had had a long night, and it wasn’t the mirror.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Mrs. Greco sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over her own parlor like a stranger’s. ¶ The cushion by the radiator was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the card party in the Greco flat at eight. Mrs. Greco had given me their names. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

Getting to Sokol’s meant a couple of blocks west. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was a cigar box under the till for lottery slips, which the barman calls receipts. ¶ Sokol was slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. Miss Lowenthal was drinking tea from a cup with a saucer, always the saucer. Doyle was handing out cigars with the alderman’s name on the band. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at nine, ten and eleven, and that Mrs. Pomerantz was with her at the Greco flat at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “A man drinks the same thing on the same stool every night of his life. When the stool is empty, I notice. When a stranger sits on it, I notice twice.” ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

It was no distance to the flats over Lipsky’s: round the corner, and there it was. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was the coal bin in the cellar, padlocked, with a chalk tally on the wall of whose scuttle got what, and two of the tallies rubbed out by a thumb. ¶ Wojcik was sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “The stoop has five steps, and the fourth one rings when you stand on it. I don’t fix it.” ¶ There was the boiler in the cellar, which the janitor speaks of as a difficult woman, and which knocks on the pipes whenever her name comes up.

Miss Nowak had told me Sokol’s at eleven, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. It was time she heard about the other one. I took the chair beside her without asking. I’d stopped being company. ¶ “You told me Sokol’s at eleven,” I said. “I wrote it down. Sokol had Mrs. Pomerantz, Doyle and Fishel at Sokol’s at eleven o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ She closed her eyes for a second, like somebody hearing a bill read out that she’d known was coming. “I’ll tell you. Only please don’t tell Mrs. Rafferty; she’s got a page for me already. I wasn’t at Sokol’s. I was at the stock room at the Peacock, with Glick. Ask him.” ¶ That was a hole in Miss Nowak’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, she had been at the stock room at the Peacock at eleven, not at Sokol’s. ¶ It turned out Glick was in the corner, out of the light.

From there to Belkin’s place was a few blocks. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ Steam heat is the whole reason anybody pays what they pay to live in the Excelsior’s flats, and against the cold the lobby was warm enough to make your nose run. A row of brass mailboxes with little windows showed who had letters and who had bills. Upstairs a phonograph was playing the same record for the third time, to somebody who didn’t care for it. There was a tall mirror in the lobby, so that everybody who comes in meets somebody who looks worse. ¶ Belkin was in the chair with the head to one side, like somebody dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. He had his greasepaint still on and a program in his coat pocket, signed to himself. ¶ Mrs. Blau, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

A few blocks uptown, and I was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ Every radiator in the flats over Lipsky’s had gone cold, and somebody on the fourth floor was banging one with a shoe, a message the janitor could read from the cellar and was choosing not to. Frost had made ferns on the shop window, over a bolt of blue serge marked down twice. There were the iron shutters on the cloth shop, which come down at suppertime with a crash the whole street hears and go up in the morning with another. ¶ Wojcik was knocking his pipe out on his boot heel and looking at nothing. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Miss Moskin was running her lines into a hand mirror. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

I set off west for the Peacock. It was a couple of blocks. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ With the band gone home, the Peacock looked like what it was: a low cellar with a damp ceiling and the chairs upside down on the tables, smelling of gin and of lilies, the lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s. The steel door was bolted. The slot opened anyway when I knocked, which told me the doorkeeper didn’t go home either. There was the cigarette girl’s tray, Luckies and Camels on the top layer and, underneath, a layer nobody buys cigarettes from. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was explaining to a large man why he was going home. She had a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it. Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. Mrs. Sobel was drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth. Russo was sitting with his back to the wall. ¶ Miss Moskin had said she was here at eight, with Mrs. Krantz, and that was worth the walk. From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “There’s one way in and one way out, and I’m sitting in both of them.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I walked downtown to the alley at Steinmetz’s. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ The alley behind Steinmetz’s was ash cans and crates and a puddle that never dries, lit by the kitchen door when it opened and by nothing when it didn’t. Somebody had made a bench out of an oyster crate and a plank, and the cobbles round it were thick with cigarette ends, where the kitchen does its thinking. There was the swinging door to the kitchen, with a porthole in it greased over so the dining room can’t see what goes into the chops. ¶ Tierney was singing under his breath about a girl from Galway. He had hands nicked all over from the shells, and a row of rings on his little finger, none of which fit. ¶ Tierney had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

It was a few blocks from there to Doyle’s place, east, with my collar up. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Excelsior stood on East Houston Street between a bank and a bakery, six floors of yellow brick with its name over the door and a lamp either side, the kind of building that puts on a necktie for the street. The lobby was tiled in black and white like a checkerboard, and somebody’s galoshes stood by the door in the middle of a game. There was a wooden wedge holding the front door open an inch for whichever tenant has lost his key this week. ¶ Doyle was on the floor, face up, with one arm flung out and the eyes on the ceiling. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ My client, Belkin, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in his hand. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I walked uptown and west to Sokol’s. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was a radio on the shelf behind the bar, turned low so the music won’t get into the bread. ¶ Sokol was rubbing his eyes with the heels of both hands, like a man trying to put them back. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Dr. Hirsch was reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead. Mrs. Greco was telling her beads with flour still on her hands. Teitel was nursing a glass of tea at the bar and telling the barman about his feet. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.” ¶ My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

Sokol’s list had Mrs. Greco here at seven, eight and ten. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. I took the stool next to her. She had a gold crucifix on a chain, and a burn on the inside of her wrist the shape of a ladle’s rim. ¶ I asked Mrs. Greco to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ She minded a little, then decided it was cheaper not to. ¶ “My night. I was on my feet. Write that down first. I was at Sokol’s from seven through eight. At seven it was just me; Dr. Hirsch and Doyle were there at eight. Then at nine I went round to Rafferty’s to borrow a collar stud, with Teitel. Come ten, I went to Sokol’s to hear the fight on the radio, with Teitel. Ten, the day should be over, and the day doesn’t listen. Walking over to Sokol’s at ten I passed Mrs. Krantz on East Houston Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten, with Teitel, and here at seven, which was what Sokol had. One evening that held, at an hour that mattered, where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. East Houston Street was where Doyle lived. ¶ Flour gets on everybody who goes through to the bar, and the whole block could find Sokol’s by the white footprints, the police included.

Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ She took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order. I was home at seven. At eight I dropped a parcel off at Rafferty’s, with Teitel. Nine o’clock I went home to iron a shirt for the morning, and stayed the rest of the evening. Nine is a good hour for rent: people are fed, and home, and feeling guilty. At seven, nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ Mrs. Krantz said home at ten. Mrs. Greco passed her on East Houston Street at ten. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. The rest held where I could check it: Teitel had her at Rafferty’s at eight, same as she said. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had said she was here at nine, and that was worth the walk to the card room over Feingold’s garage. ¶ Winding her watch at the kitchen table, slowly, like a duty: that was the last I saw of her.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. My visitor talked the whole walk to the chair: her sister, her landlord, and eventually the reason she’d come. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Frieda Kahane. Hyman Glick’s neighbor, or I was till tonight, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Glick had been the insurance agent, and was found dead in his own flat in the Belvedere on Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The one who found the body was Mrs. Blau, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When did it happen?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” Miss Kahane said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening it was Sokol’s,” she said. “The usual. You could have set a clock by it.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad of it?” ¶ “I found a letter from Miss Moskin in the desk,” she said. “He was squeezing Miss Moskin’s boss for money. Start there.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Miss Kahane said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I put the money in my wallet, where it looked lonely and slightly surprised.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through the papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Miss Moskin: an IOU from her boss, with her name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Ostrow: a sealed envelope with her name on it. Belkin: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Miss Nowak: a note about her and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Mrs. Blau: a clipping about her, with a remark pencilled across it. ¶ A reason is the easy half. Everybody in Glick’s box had one. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

Wojcik’s list had Miss Moskin here at seven. That was reason enough to ask. ¶ She was running her lines into a hand mirror. She had a copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ She didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “Oh, my evening. Let me do it properly. You have to set the scene, or it doesn’t play. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven, with Miss Nowak. Seven’s my nervous hour. Every actress has one, and mine’s at seven. At eight I stopped in at Sokol’s to get warm, with Mrs. Ostrow. Nine o’clock I went to the kitchen at Steinmetz’s for a late plate. Then at ten I turned in early, home at the flats over Lipsky’s. I had nobody with me at nine or ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Miss Moskin said the kitchen at Steinmetz’s at nine and home at ten. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ Doing her stretching exercises on the landing, to the annoyance of the stairs: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Miss Kahane had said nine or ten o’clock. The rat poison had come from the flats over Lipsky’s. I had an evening from Miss Moskin, and a list from Wojcik. I didn’t have Mrs. Ostrow’s, Miss Nowak’s, Belkin’s or Mrs. Blau’s evenings yet. ¶ That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

Miss Moskin had said Miss Nowak was with her at her place at seven, and I wanted the rest of that evening. ¶ The woman with a cane was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. She had nails painted red and bitten, both. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. At seven I went to the flats over Lipsky’s for the company, and stayed through nine. Miss Moskin was there at seven; Belkin and Mrs. Blau were there at eight; Mrs. Blau was there at nine. Eight’s when I feel lucky. I don’t know why. It’s cost me a fortune. Come ten, I went to Sokol’s to see who was in, by myself.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Nowak said Sokol’s. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline.

I walked east to Belkin’s flat. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Rain on East Houston Street, which is wide enough to rain on properly. The lobby of the Excelsior had a rubber mat inside the door and a sign above it asking tenants please to use it, with the please underlined twice, which tells you how that was going. There was a dumbwaiter in the back hall for coal and parcels, with a bell on every floor that nobody answers. ¶ Belkin, in a green hat, was telling a story about Odessa in 1899. He had a ring on every finger but one, and a pale band of skin on that one. ¶ Miss Nowak had said Belkin was with her at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. I had no plans for bed and had stopped pretending otherwise. I kept the lamp burning for the company more than the light. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Pickering said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I got up and offered him the chair, and he sat down in it carefully, the way people sit in chairs they don’t trust. ¶ “I sat in Moe’s from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Eveready Hour, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “There’s Marchetti,” he said. “I don’t like gossip, but he and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ He looked at the window, then back at me. “Dettweiler, an insurance agent, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what the cigarette case was worth. And Hochstetter, a night-school teacher, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ Pickering counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

It was a few blocks to Moe’s, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The stars were out over the rooftops, which in this city means somebody forgot to switch something on. ¶ Moe’s, a back-room bar behind a cigar store, was one room with no windows, a curtain for a door and a bar along one wall. After midnight it had the quiet of a place that expects to be quiet and is paid to be. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Weisglass was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Marchetti was in a booth by the wall, alone with a glass of beer and a newspaper. Hochstetter was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it. ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

I walked west to Rafferty’s. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ I went up the stoop at Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street. It was four floors of narrow rooms and one long stair, with a gas lamp on each landing turned down to a little blue bead. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Dettweiler was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Salerno was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ Hochstetter had said he was here at nine, with Salerno. It was reason enough to look. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. The retainer was still folded in my breast pocket. I’d checked for it twice on the walk up, which wasn’t like me. I put it in the drawer, where it would keep its shape better than I would. ¶ The street door went downstairs, and somebody started up, taking the stairs slowly, like somebody not sure they were the right stairs. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “It’s a set of silver spoons,” Ainsworth said. “It was in the velvet box in the sideboard drawer, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I got up and offered her the chair, and she sat down in it carefully, the way people sit in chairs they don’t trust. ¶ “I sat in the chop house from eight until ten,” she said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ “And I know when,” she said. “The dog next door went off at ten o’clock, the way it does when somebody’s on the stairs.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “It’s Salerno,” Ainsworth said. “She stood at my elbow at the chop house the whole time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the spoons would pawn for.” ¶ She looked at the window, then back at me. “Hauck, a switchboard operator, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what the spoons was worth. And Marchetti, a milliner, always said the spoons was wasted on me.” ¶ Ten dollars came out of a pocket that had been saving it for something better. “Find out who. And get the spoons back.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

The chop house was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door, and the soup had been crossed out. ¶ Havemeyer was going from table to table with a cloth over his arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Hauck sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. ¶ A head waiter shows everybody to a table, so Havemeyer would know who had come in tonight and where they’d been put. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

The Delmonico rooms were a couple of blocks downtown. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Ruggiero sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Salerno was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Feldman was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ Hauck had said she was here at eight, and that Salerno was with her at the chop house at nine. That settled where I was going. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Ruggiero had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I walked uptown and east to the Petrosino flat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ The Petrosino parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Petrosino showed me where the brooch had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If it went at ten, it went after the meeting, and everybody at the meeting had known the way in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Abramowitz. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I asked Abramowitz where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. He didn’t like being asked, and didn’t pretend to. ¶ “I was at Petrosino’s at eight, for the meeting, with Fairbanks and Donnelly. Nine o’clock I left the meeting when the gin ran out and went home to listen to the radio, and stayed through ten. Donnelly was there at nine; at ten it was just me. Then at eleven I couldn’t settle, so I went to the chop house for coffee, with Donnelly and Wehrle.” ¶ So the Petrosino flat at eight, with Fairbanks and Donnelly, which was what Petrosino had said. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said home at Mrs. Nagy’s. That was his word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ Broadnax would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ The slate by the door promised a lot and had crossed out the best of it, like most menus and most evenings.

I kept my voice down. Fairbanks kept his eyes on me. ¶ I said it plainly. “Broadnax has you at the chop house at nine. So where were you the rest of the night?” He counted back through the evening under his breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I was at Petrosino’s at eight, for the meeting, with Donnelly and Abramowitz. Come nine, I left the meeting to get some air and went to the chop house to read the late paper over a plate of soup, and stayed through ten. Around eleven I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning. At nine, ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ Fairbanks said the chop house at ten. Broadnax had Donnelly, Wehrle and Lou at the chop house at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. The rest held where I could check it: Petrosino had him at the Petrosino flat at eight, with Abramowitz, same as he said. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Fairbanks, Donnelly and Abramowitz were at the meeting and knew the way in; Wehrle wasn’t. Fairbanks had told me the chop house at ten, and Broadnax’s list said otherwise. Donnelly was at the chop house at ten; Broadnax said so. Abramowitz said home at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. Wehrle was at the chop house at ten; Broadnax said so. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the chop house at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s who’d been in. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

From there to Mrs. Nagy’s was a long walk. The fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ I went to Mrs. Nagy’s rooms on East Fourth Street. It was a tall thin house that leaned a little on its neighbor, like a lodger who has had one too many. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

I walked east to Tramonti’s place. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ I went to Tramonti’s rooms behind the tailor’s on Allen Street. The passage from Allen Street smelled of pressed wool and machine oil, and it ended at a door the police had pulled shut on their way out. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Tramonti lay on the floor on one side, where the fall had left the body, with the knees drawn up a little. ¶ Winslow was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ Nobody kept watch there. It wasn’t that kind of place. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

From there to the Orpheum was a couple of blocks. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Hochstetter was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Carbone was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Fairbanks was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. Weisglass sat in the back row with his hat on his knee, watching the picture without looking at it. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Hochstetter. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Rafferty’s was a couple of blocks uptown and west. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Thorndike was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ Carbone had said he was here at seven. Hochstetter’s list had Thorndike at the Orpheum at seven. That was reason enough. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Rafferty had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

A fair few blocks east, and I was at Sokol’s back room. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ The back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken, smelled of rye bread and pencil shavings. A bakery makes its money in the morning, and the back room made its money all night, a nickel at a time. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Vogel was at a table by the ovens, sorting slips of paper into piles by number. She had a good hat and cheap shoes, and was up on her toes the whole time, ready to be somewhere else. ¶ Whoever takes the slips sees everybody who puts down a nickel, and everybody does. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.
